ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
National Population Policy 
*261. SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the policy laid down by the National Commission on Population 
towards a stable and sustainable population size; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the National Population Policy (NPP) desires 
to bring the Total Fertility Rate (TFR) to the replacement level of 2.10 by the year 
2010; 
(c) whether it would be possible with this TFR of 2.10 to restrict the 
National Population to 1107 million by 2010 A.D.; and 
(d) whether it is also a fact that the Planning Commission has set a target 
of population growth of 16.2 percent between 2001 and 2011 in the Tenth Five 
Year Plan, implying a population of 1193 million? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PL ANNING (SHRI 
SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of 
the House. 
2 

[7 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Statement 
(a) The policy towards a stable and sustainable population size has 
been laid down in the National Population Policy (NPP) 2000. The salient 
features of NPP are inter alia: 
(i) address the unmet needs for basic reproductive and child health 
services, supplies and infrastructure, 
(ii) promote delayed marriage for girls not earlier than age 18 and 
preferably after 20 years of age, 
(iii) achieve universal access to information/counselling and services for 
fertility regulation and contraception with a wide basket of choices, 
(iv) promote vigorously the small family norm to achieve replacement 
levels of TFR. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) No, Sir. The NPP projected the population for 2010 to reach 1107 
million if TFR of 2.1 is achieved by that year on the basis of 1991 Census data. 
However, the 2001 Census has shown th at the actual population is greater 
than the NPP projections for 2001. 
(d) Yes, Sir. 
SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN: Mr. Chairman, Sir, India, perhaps, is the first 
country among the developing countries in the world, which has l aunched the 
Family Planning Programme as back as in 1952. Since t hen, we have made 
many statements; particularly, the Government of India has come out with 
many policy documents and statements. In 1976...

Governments should also take steps to see that the target is achieved and

Ban on Pakistani newspapers 
*262. SHRIMATI BIMBA RAIKAR: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is a continued mutual ban in India and Pakistan on each 
other's newspapers; and 
(b) whether as a logical follow-up of Delhi-Lahore Bus Service and restoration of 
airline flights between India and Pakistan, India would take the initiative in lifting the 
ban on Pakistani newspapers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI 
DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) Government of India does not discriminate against Pakistan in 
the import of newspapers. Import of printed material from Pakistan continues to be 
permitted. General restrictions on the import of seditious, inflammatory or obscene 
material from any foreign country apply in case of Pakistan also. According to available 
information, Pakistan does not permit the import of newspapers from India. 
(b) Does not arise.

Bangalore

Rail link between New Delhi and Hanoi 
*263. SHRI LALIT SURI: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Myanmar Foreign Minister, at a recent meeting 
of Mekong-Ganga Cooperation Group held at Phnom Penh, made a proposal 
for a rail link between New Delhi and Hanoi; 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) whether any agency has been identified for conducting feasibility study 
of the project, if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI VINOD KHANNA): (a) At their Mi nisterial meeting in Phnom Penh in 
June, 2003, the Mekong-Ganga Cooperat ion (MGC) countries have agreed to 
study the feasibility of establishing a rail link between New Delhi and Hanoi. 
(b) Government fully support this initiative and have offered to send a team 
of experts to carry out a preliminary study in this regard. 
(c) No, Sir. 
8 

[7 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
SHRI LALIT SURI: Mr. Chairman, Sir. seeing the importance of 
connectivity between New Delhi and Hanoi, this will be one of the greatest links in 
South-East Asia comparable to the Trans-Siberian Railway and the European 
rail network. This will boost the economy by way of easy accessibility for goods 
to be transported as well as tourism. I would like to ask of the hon. Minister: Is 
the Government appointing a joint working and a specialised agency to study 
and take advantage of the successful network of the Trans-Siberian railway and 
European rail for the successful implementation of this linkage? 
SHRI VINOD KHANNA: Sir, I should like to emphasise that the proposal is at a 
very preliminary stage. The MGC Ministers have agreed that it would be a good idea 
to explore the feasibility of such a link. India has offered to depute a team to make 
a preliminary study. But the terms of reference as well as the agency for 
undertaking this study remain still to be identified. 
SHRI LALIT SURI: Sir, my second supplementary is this. Which countries 
are participating in this project and will the Government find any difficulty to 
include Bangladesh in this project so as to make it viable by a reduction of a few 
hundreds of kilometres in route as compared to the North-Eastern route which 
will be long and has a difficult terrain? 
SHRI VINOD KHANNA: Sir, the MGC countries comprise Cambodia, Laos, 
Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam and India. So as far as Bangladesh is concerned, 
because of its geographical position, it has an important  role in this matter. 
However, it has not been responsive to India's longstanding requests of transit 
facilities to strengthen the transport linkages between the North-Eastern Region 
and the rest of India. I hope, some day, wisdom will dawn.

*268.  SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: †† 
SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: 
Will the Minister of LABOUR be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the avenues for employment are shrinking and the 
number of unemployed and semi-employed persons are soaring over the years; 
(b) the generation of employment opportunities planned in different 
categories during the period 2003-04 and 2004-05; 
(c) what has been and what is likely to be the impact of cut in jobs in 
Government PSUs, divestment in PSUs and closure of industrial units in creating 
new job opportunities; and 
(d) whether Government have set any target to provide employment to 
every eligible citizen of the country? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (SHRI SAHIB SINGH VERMA): (a) to (d) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a to d) Estimates of employment and unemployment are obtained through 
quinquennial labour force surveys conducted by National Sample Survey 
Organisation. Last such survey was conducted during 1999-2000. As per 
these surveys, estimated employment in  the country on usual status basis has 
gone up from approximately 374 million in 1993-94 to 397 million on 1999-2000. 
Number of unemployed during 1993-94 and 1999-2000 was approximately 75 
lakh and 90 lakh respectively. 
The Special Group headed by Dr. S.  P. Gupta, Member, Planning 
Commission has recommended strategy and programmes which have been 
considered while formulating the 10th Plan, for targeting creation of 50 million 
employment opportunities (10 million per year) during the 10th Plan period 
(2002-2007). It identified the activities where there is a major potential of large 
new job opportunities as in agricultur e, including social forestry, animal 
husbandry, fishing, horticulture and related areas and small and medium 
industries, construction, tourism, information

that with the target of achieving 10 millio n jobs per year, it will be possible to

country. Loss of jobs, if any, in Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs), disinvested 
PSUs and industrial units, may not have any significant effect on total 
employment in the country.

Statement 
Some of the important findings of C and AG 
55. Quality of services of Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Limited. 
55.1 Summary of important findings and Highlights; 
MTNL has been providing various basic and value added services to 
subscribers through its networks in Delhi and Mumbai. In a majority of cases 
there have been abnormal delays vis-a-vis norms prescribed in providing 
services to subscribers, which led to dissatisfaction and inconvenience to them. 
Delays were specially long in the case of shifting of telephones, telephone transfer 
to another person's name and clearance of telephone faults. MTNL has not even 
fixed norms/targets for providing certain services. Even its comparative 
performance in providing services to different areas of Delhi varied considerably: 
the best quality of service was provided to Central Area, while the East Area 
received the worst. In a majority of cases the quality of services was poor on 
account of insufficient coordination. The overall quality of various services 
provided by MTNL, remained below average. 
Some of the important findings are highlighted below: 
 In case of Mumbai unit, the percent age of execution of OBs within the 
prescribed norm of 15 days increased from 52 per cent in 1998-99 to 
64 per cent in 1999-2000 but thereafter declined to 50 per

execution of OBs within the 15 days norm increased from 13 per cent

not fall within the category of 'strategic sector and hence, that the Government

approved the sale of 72% equity in favour of M/s Ruia Cotex Ltd. (consortium)

of India were transparent.The Division Bench of Kolkata High Court rejected the 
prayer for stay of the judgement so ught by the Jessop and Co. Ltd. Staff

Support to India's cause against cross border terrorism 
1985. SHRI LALIT SURI: Will the Mi nister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether there was any significant indication to help India's cause against 
cross border terrorism by Pakistan during the recent discussions of Deputy 
Prime Minister with the President of United States of America and the Prime 
Minister of United Kingdom; and 
(b) what follow up action is being taken by Government to help India's cause 
on the issue? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) The U.S. President and the U.K. Prime Minister 
conveyed to the Deputy Prime Minister, during his visit to USA and UK in June 
2003; that they would cont inue to press Pakistan to fulfil its commitments on 
crossborder terrorism. 
(b) Government believes that Indi a is fully capable of combating 
crossborder terrorism on its own. At t he same time, Government continues its 
purposive engagement with the international community, which has led to 
widespread international recognition of Pakistan's responsibility to take steps 
for bringing an end to crossborder terrorism in India.

Pak failure to stop terrorism 
†1986. SHRIMATI MAYA SINGH: W ill the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Presid ent of Pakistan has categorically stated 
during the visit to his country by the leaders from abroad and during his own 
visit to foreign countries, that he cannot stop terrorism going on in Jammu and 
Kashmir, completely; 
(b) if so, whether it would adversely affect the peace talk to be held 
between the two countries; and 
(c) if so, Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) Contrary to  facts, the President of Pakistan, 
General Musharraf, has from time to  time claimed inter alia that nothing was 
happening across the Line of Control, Pakistan had done all it could, or 
suggested that Pakistani State or agencies were not behind the terrorists acting 
against India. 
(b) and (c) President Musharraf's comments are clearly unhelpful in the 
context of Prime Minister's initiative to establish trust and confidence in India-
Pakistan relations. 
Government have made it clear that creation of conducive atmosphere for 
a sustained dialogue necessarily required an end to cross border terrorism 
and dismantling of the infrastructure of support to terrorism in Pakistan.

Break-through due to step by step approach with Pakistan 
1988. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: W ill the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether step by step approach of India with Pakistan has been on for 
quite some time; 
133 

RAJYA SABHA [7 August, 2003] 
(b) if so, the break-through made in this direction; 
(c) whether the said approach is playing any role in the engagement 
between India and Pakistan; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) to (d) Prime Minister had, on April 18, 2003, 
once again extended the hand of friendship to Pakistan. In his statement in 
Parliament on May 2, he had announced the decision to appoint a High 
Commissioner to Pakistan and to restore civil aviation links on a reciprocal 
basis. It had also been made clear that India would pursue a step-by-step 
approach to normalisation of links and that  creating conditions conducive to 
sustained dialogue necessarily required an  end to cross-border infiltration and 
dismantling of the infrastructure of support to terrorism in Pakistan. Subsequently, 
on May 26, Government indicated its willingness for the resumption of Delhi-
Lahore bus service. 
Following Prime Minister's initiative both countries have appointed High 
Commissioners. The Delhi-Lahore bus service has been resumed with effect 
from July 11. Technical level discussions for resumption of civil aviation are 
scheduled to be held on August 27-28,2003. Both sides have released prisoner. 
There have also been important exchanges in the context of business, cultural 
and people-to-people contacts. 
India is committed to resolving all outstanding issues with Pakistan 
peacefully through direct bilateral dialogue in the spirit of Simla Agreement and 
Lahore Declaration. Government intends to proceed with present approach of 
step-by-step normalization of diplomatic and other links. Further steps would 
be considered based on the progress made, and confidence generated.

(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) to (d) In accordance with the Simla Agreement of 
1972, a Protocol on Resumption of Trade was signed by India and Pakistan on

economic relations if it is to be seen to be committed to improving bilateral and 
regional economic cooperation.

2072. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of steps that have been taken to offset the trend of 
sickness in the SSI sector; and 
(b) the steps that have been taken to rehabilitate SSI units in the 
country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES (SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR): (a) and (b) The number of sick Small 
Scale Industries (SSIs) has declined from 3,06,221 as at the end of March, 
1999 to 1,77,336 as at the end of March, 2002 as per the latest data compiled 
by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) from Scheduled Commercial Banks. 
The Government is fully seized of the problem of industrial sickness 
amogst the SSI units and has taken various steps to facilitate timely 
identification and rehabilitation of potentially viable sick industries including 
institutional mechanism in the form of State-level Inter-Institutional 
Committees, Special Rehabilitation Ce lls in banks and State Financial 
Institutions. Elaborate guidelines have been issued by the Reserve Bank of 
India for extending rehabilitation assistance to eligible units. Further, based on 
the recommendations of the Working Group set up under the Chairmanship of 
Shri S.S. Kohli, the RBI has drawn up re vised guidelines for rehabilitation of 
sick SSI units, which include inter-alia change in the definition of sick SSI 
units, norms for deciding on their viability, concessional finance, etc. The RBI 
has circulated the revised guidelines on 16th January, 2002 to all the 
scheduled commercial banks for implementation. 
203 

RAJYA  SABHA [7 August, 2003] 
Recession in SSI sector 
2073. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGAR WALLA: Will the Minister of 
SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that many small scale industrial units 
are facing unprecedented recession; and 
(b) if so, what steps are taken by Government to revive small scale units 
and to boost their performance? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES (SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR): (a) While the annual growth rate of Small 
Scale Industries (SSIs) Sector declined from 8.23 per cent in 2000-01 to 6.08 
per cent in 2001-02, the same is estima ted to have increased to 7.41 per cent 
in 2002-03. The downtrend in 2001-02 could be partly due to overall 
recessionary trend in the industrial sector. 
(b) To strengthen and enhance the competitiveness of the SSI Sector, both 
domestically and globally, the Government has taken various measures, which 
include enhancement of working capital limit computed on the basis of minimum 
of 20% of annual projected.turnover from Rs. 4 crore to Rs. 5 crore, 
enhancement in composite loan limit from Rs. 10 lakhs to Rs. 25 lakhs, raising 
of project cost limit under National Equity Fund Scheme from Rs. 25 lakhs to Rs. 
50 lakhs, revision in eligible loan limit for coverage under Credit Guarantee 
Scheme from Rs. 10 lakhs to Rs. 25 lakhs, introduction of Laghu Udyami Credit 
Card (LUCC) Scheme, issuance of revised guidelines for rehabilitation of sick 
SSI units and revival of potentially viable units, by the Reserve Bank of India on 
16th January, 2002, etc. Further, in accordance with the announcement made 
in the Union Budget 2003-04, the Indian Banks' Association has advised all its 
member banks to adopt an interest rate bank of 2 per cent above and below 
Prime Lending Rate (PLR) as announced by  the State Bank of India. Banks 
have also agreed to further raise the composite loan limit from Rs. 25 lakhs to 
Rs. 50 lakhs.

SHRI P. G. NARAYANAN (Tamil Nadu): Madam, in pursuance to the 
recommendations of the Committee on Pr evention of Corruption headed by 
Shri Santanam, the CVC was set up in the year 1994 through a Resolution. 
The said Resolution provided that t he Central Vigilance Commissioner would 
be attached to the Ministry of Home Affair s. But, in exercise of its powers and 
functions, it will not be subordinate to any Ministry and it will have the same 
measure of independence and autonom y as the Union Public Service 
Commission has. In September, 1997, the Government constituted an 
independent Review Committee, comprisi ng of Shri P. G. Deshmukh, Shri V. 
V. Giri and Shri N. N. Vohra, to suggest measures for strengthening anti-
corruption activities as part of its efforts against corruption. One of the 
recommendations made by the Committee was the conferment of statutory 
status on the CVC, along with the restor ation of the provision relating to the 
appointment of the Central Vigila nce Commission. The Committee had also 
recommended that the CVC should be made responsible for the efficient 
functioning of the CBI. 
223 

RAJYA SABHA [7 August, 2003] 
Subsequently, the hon. Supreme Court, in the year 1997, in Vineet 
Narain's case - which is, probably, known as the Jain Hawala Case -- had 
given the direction that statutory status should be conferred on the CVC. 
Then, in the year 1998, two Ordinances  had been promulgated to comply with 
the directions of the Supreme Cour t; and, subsequently, the Bill was 
introduced in the Lok Sabha. The 12 th Lok Sabha was dissolved on 26 th April, 
1999 and, consequently, the CVC Bill l apsed. The Supreme Court judgment 
had declared the singular directive null and void. The singular directive was a 
set of Executive instructions issued by the Central Government, prohibiting the 
CBI from undertaking any inquiry or inve stigation against any officer of the 
rank of Joint Secretary and above in the Central Government, without prior 
sanction of the Head of Department. The Court found it bad in law on two 
grounds -- one, it required Police to seek permission from the Executive to 
initiate investigation into a criminal offence; two, it vi olated the canon of 
equality in the application of law. T he exemption -- extended to the senior 
officers from even being enquired into by the CBI without the Government's 
permission -- is now being accorded legal sanctity. The Committee has tried to 
justify the restoration of this single directive on the ground that no protection is 
available to the person at the highest decision-making level. It is noteworthy to 
mention that the protection against the prosecution, without the sanction of the 
Government, is already available to all public servants under Section 197 of the 
Criminal Procedure Code and Section 19 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. 
Madam, even Kautilya, in his Arthashastra, says that it is not possible to 
stop fish from drinking water. So, corru ption has always been a part of our 
public life. This position has to change. Corruption has to be fought because it 
is anti-poor, anti-nationa l and anti-economic development. In brief, the CVC 
should be given statutory power, and the provision of the Bill is to be 
implemented in letter and spirit to elim inate the cancerous corruption from our 
system

experience as to what should be done to strengthen the vigilance mechanism 
to deal with Civil Servants' corruption. 
Madam, within the short time that is available to me, I can only touch 
on two or three points. I would like to say that the corrupt officer is very well 
experienced in managing to escape punishment by his own efforts or by 
manipulating things in such a way that  the punishment remains uninfected till 
he leaves the service. If you take the hi story of investigations or inquiries 
against the Civil Servants on corruption charges, you will be amazed to find 
how few among those who have been prima facie charged with offences have 
ultimately been punished. If in certain cases a Civil Servant succeeds to go 
outside the service by resigning or opting for retirement, he would have 
manipulated things in such a way that for him it is not a punishment but a 
reward. The built-in provisions of inquiry, appeal and final review by the 
appointing authority are such that they always favour the person who want to 
escape punishment. Therefore, what is needed in an effective instrument 
against corruption in our country, as fa r as Civil Servants are concerned, is a 
change or a reform in the procedures of  inquiry, investigation, punishment, 
appeal and final award of punishment.

escape punishment. These are the two important reasons.   There

time he is booked in a corruption case and if he has to be prosecuted or an 
inquiry itself has to be conducted only after sanction or approval by the 
Government, we are really offering a shelter to the person who has now 
become a real source of corruption in bureaucracy.    This is my second point. 
When I entered the civil service way back in 1948. at the beginning 
of our Independence, my worry was whether my Tehsildaar would be corrupt, 
my Sub-Inspector would be corrupt, the Bench Clerk in my court would be 
corrupt. I could never imagine that my senior officers would be corrupt. I could 
never imagine when I became a senior officer that I would ever become 
corrupt. Today you ask junior officers in any service, including the All-India 
Services like IPS and IAS and they will point the finger right up to the top and 
say, "These are the people sitting in the Secretariat, heading the Department, 
who are more corrupt than us". What have we done under this Bid? We have 
given them protection. A Government  sanction is needed before an inquiry 
can be started. 
239 

RAJYA SABHA [7 August, 2003] 
Who are the people who will decide in the Government whether an 
inquiry should be started or not? Are they Ministers who are going to take a 
decision? If it is the Minister, how will  he be able to decide whether there is a 
prima facie case against a Joint Secretary or an Additional Secretary, unless 
there is an inquiry? But the language of the Bill is such that even to start an 
inquiry, even to find out whether there is a prima facie case or not, you have to 
take permission. Therefore, there is go ing to be a lot of arbitrariness, 
highhandedness and, if I may say so, favouritism and cronyism involved in 
allowing prosecution or inquiry. This is a very serious matter. Therefore, I 
would very strongly suggest that clause 6 (a) should be deleted from the Bill. 
The delays that occur in sanctioning or approving an inquiry will be a case 
study worth making by anyone else. I had done it myself. I know, very often, 
whenever there is a sanction to be obtained, the whole thing can be delayed 
for not months, but years together. T herefore, clause 6 (a) which has been 
introduced in the Bill, I consider, as the enemy number one for this Bill. It will 
lengthen the procedure, defeat the obj ective and make the corrupt breathe 
free than what they could have normally done. Madam, I will also make one or 
two small points. I want to find out why clause 5 (9) (3) has been added in the 
Bill at all. It says that the business of t he Commission shall, as far as possible, 
be transacted through unanimity. I couldn't understand, having created a 
Commission of three people, why we should insist on unanimity among the 
three. Even though we have added the words 'as far as possible', This is going 
to be a Pandora's box. If the Commission comes to a decision that 'X' is 
punishable for a particular offence, and if there is no unanimity, the person 
concerned is going to exploit that; he will go on appeal, drag the whole 
procedure to all the courts that he can, have an opportunity of getting it open, 
and it will lead to unnecessary and vexatious delay. If a High Court Bench can 
take decisions affecting life and property, liberty and rights on majority 
principle, if the Supreme Court takes decision on a majority "basis, then, why 
should we introduce this unanimity concept? Even though there is a clause 
saying, "as far as possible, there should be unanimity", it may be a small point 
in the eyes of others, but it has to be, in my judgement, deleted. 
Finally, I would say, Madam, I endorse the very valuable suggestion 
you made in the morning that in making the selections for the Chief Vigilance 
Commissioner and others, the Leader of the Opposition in the Rajya Sabha 
also should find a place in the selection board. This should not be a matter left 
entirely to the Constitution, as It is proposed in the Bill, where there is no 
provision for a representation by the Rajya Sabha. 
240 

[7 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Madam, I know that the time that has been allotted to me is only 
three or four minutes, and out of your generosity and kindness, you have been 
looking the other way, but I have been looking at the watch, and I am coming

Sir, the idea for a Central Vigilance Commission had been mooted in 
early sixties, when the Santhanam Committee exposed the weaknesses in 
fighting the menace of corruption in  administration. The Santhanam 
Committee pointed out that the administration could not be a judge of its own 
conduct. Hence, the Central Vigilance Commission was conceptualised as an 
apex body for exercising general superintendence and control over vigilance 
matters in administration. 
After the directions given by the Supreme Court in the Vineet 
Narayan case and other havala cases, the Central Vigilance Commission was 
given statutory status through an Or dinance in 1998. Then, the Central 
Vigilance Commission Bill, 1998, was introduced in the Lok Sabha and was 
passed in March, 1999, but was pending before the Rajya Sabha. 
As the earlier Ordinance of 1998 expired, and the Bill was also not 
adopted in Parliament, a new Ordinance had to be promulgated. Then, the 
Union Government resolved on 4.4. 1999, that the Central Vigilance 
Commission constituted under the Ordinance would continue to discharge its 
duties and exercise its powers under the same resolution of 4.4.1999, after 
the expiry of the 1999 Ordinance. 
The Government, once again, introduced the Central Vigilance 
Commission Bill, 1999, in the Lok Sabha, which was referred to a Joint 
Committee of both Houses of Parliament. All these delayed exercises create 
confusion in the minds of the public  about the real intention of the 
Government to fight against the rampant corruption in the higher bureaucratic 
echelons of the Government.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI 1.0. SWAMI) : Madam, I move: 
That the Bill to provide for the transfer for certain prisoners from India 
to country or place outside India and reception in India of certain 
prisoners from country or place outside India, as passed by Lok 
Sabha, be taken into consideration. 
Presently, as the august House knows, there is no legal provision in 
the CrPC and there is no other law wh ereby we can transport or repatriate 
prisoners languishing in jails in other countries and vice-versa. Most of the 
prisoners who are here in our jails also cannot be transferred to other 
countries because there is no law at present. In the absence of the legislative 
provision, it has become almost im possible to execute treaties and 
agreements with foreign Governments for transfer of convicted persons. The 
sentence awarded by foreign courts c annot be acted upon under the existing 
laws. The proposed legislation in conjuction with bilateral agreements or 
treaties would certainly enable this Government to transfer the foreign 
convicted offenders to the countries of their origin and receive the Indian 
citizens serving sentences and languishing for a long time in jails of other 
countries. This provision shall apply to  the enforcement of sentences imposed 
before as well as after the enactment of this law. 
Madam, this is a happy note t hat the Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Home Affairs, to whom this Bill was referred to by this House, 
has discussed this Bill clause-by-claus e in its meetings and sought some 
clarifications from the Ministry.    After those clarifications were given,

and Agreements and repatriation of Indian prisoners in the jails of foreign

to be signed. With five other countries, we  are in the proces of negotiation. All

2003, which has been passed by the Lok Sabha, is being placed before this 
House for its consideration so that this Bill is considered and passed.

SHRI I.D. SWAMI : Sir, I am grateful to all the hon. Members who 
have participated in this debate. I am ve ry happy that almost all the Members 
have not only welcomed the Bill but  have agreed that it has humane 
dimensions also. All these things have been kept in view while drafting this 
Bill. Some of the questions which have been raised may be they are not very 
relevant to the Bill but all the same they do concern this country, they do 
create anxiety in the minds of the hon. members. I would also like to address 
those anxieties of the Members. So fa r as the provisions of the law are 
concerned, the hon. Member, who spoke ju st now, has pointed out - I might 
just mention about it - that it is the intention of the Gove rnment, through this 
law, to implement the treaties and agreements which are entered into with 
foreign countries. If certain treaties or agreements are entered into with foreign 
countries, in order to comply with those treaties or to implement those 
agreements, there needed an enabling law. And the enabling law provides 
that wherever adaptability is  needed, if the nature, du ration of the sentence, 
the character of the s entence, etc., is not compatible between the two 
countries and there are minor differences, then, that country has the liberty to 
adapt that sentence. But, so far as the clemency or the remission of the 
sentence is concerned, certainly, that part of the 'jurisdiction still stays with the 
courts and with the transferring country . It was mentioned that in certain 
countries, especially, the Islamic countri es, the Gulf countries, the sentence 
could be purchased. Certainly, if th ere are such provisions, then, the 
transferring country may not agree to that transfer at all, and that is where we 
say that if at all clemency has to be show n, if at all remission is to be given, 
that will have to be given by the courts of this country or by the Government of 
this country, that is, by the Rashtrapathi  of this country. No other country can 
purchase that sentence. If we feel that the receiving country is not going to 
abide by our conditions, - at the time of  entering into treaties, there would be 
agreements, there would be conditions, and at the time of transfer of prisoners 
also, those conditions would be mentioned - only if the receiving 
300 

[7 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Government   accepts  those  conditions,   only  on  those  conditions,   the 
prisoners would be repatriated. 
So far as the powers of Joint Secretary are concerned, well, it is 
understood that so far as the warra nt of handing over of prisoners is 
concerned, those powers are being exer cised by the Joint Secretary or the 
executive authorities. But a Joint Secretary or an executive authority cannot 
change the sentence which has been given by the courts.

SHRI I.D. SWAMI: That would be done by the courts concerned. The

operation, not otherwise...

SHRI I.D. SWAMI: Before the repatriation is done, before the warrant

country, and if the transferring country, sa y, India, feels t hat their law has

framed. At the time of framing the rules, this would be decided upon.

SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE (West Be ngal): Sir, I would like to 
submit this whole thing with some background. Yesterday, we met in the 
Business Advisory Committee and gave certain suggestions to the 
Government to come out of the impasse that has been created. And, even in 
the morning, it was going on. We suggested that we would like to have a 
debate on the Report of the Public Accounts Committee and the precedents 
have also been given to the Report of the PAC being discussed. The issue, 
which has arisen, relates to the very basic, fundamental principles and duties 
in the functioning of a Parliamentary Committee. Sir, the Public Accounts 
Committee, in its Report, which has been  placed on the Table of the House, 
has alleged that certain documents, which were relevant, according to its 
judgment, for consideration of the CAG Report on "Operation Vijay", were 
not made available to it. Due to the persistent refusal of the Ministry of 
Defence to submit those documents to the PAC, it came to the conclusion that, 
in the absence of documents from the Ministry of defence, it was not in a 
position to examine the CAG Report on the "Operation Vijay." I don't 
remember whether it has ever happened. But, I do remember that in 1978, the 
Privileges Committee of the Lok Sabha accused a Prime Minister of eleven 
years' standing and just elected to th e Lok Sabha, of causing disturbance to 
and interference with the co llection of material for the consideration of the 
PAC and on that basis, dismissed her from membership and sent her to jail in 
December, 1978. Therefore, this is a serious matter. What we had submitted to 
you yesterday in the Business Adviso ry Committee was that the impasse can 
be resolved if a debate on the Repor t of the PAC takes place and the hon. 
Prime Minister, or, the Government give s an assurance that the hon. Prime 
Minister would respond to that debate. We also suggested that the relevant 
documents, which were sought by the PAC, should be given to it and the 
minutes and the verbatim record of th e PAC should also be placed on the 
Table of the House so that there is no  apprehension on any other thing. You 
also, Sir, in your wisdom, indicated that you, yourself, would like to go 
through the records. Then, we pointed out yesterday itself, with utmost 
respect, that unless these issues are clinched, it is not possible for the 
Opposition to co-operate with the Gove rnment. It is not that we are doing 
something off the cuff. Yesterday, we  made it quite clear. My friend, Mr. 
Nilotpal Basu, articulated it clearly that it is for the Government of the day to 
say whether it wants to come off the impasse that has been

sixty-first anniversary of the historic day when the Quit India Movement 
was launched by the Father of the Nation, Mahatma Gandhi, in 1942. 
There was an overwhelming response to the clarion call of Gandhiji. 
Men, women, and even children came out in large numbers to participate 
in the movement with total dedication and commitment. This 
spontaneous upsurge of nationalistic sentiments culminated later, after 
five years, in our attaining Independence. 
We pay our respectful tributes to the martyrs who sacrificed their 
lives and to those who had undergone untold sufferings for the cause 
of our freedom. 
I would request Members to rise in  their places and observe silence 
as a mark of respect to the memory of the martyrs of our freedom 
struggle. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute)

occurred two minutes after the helicopter took off from the oil rig, Sagar 
Kiran, at Bombay High.The search is still on for those who are missing. 
I am sure that the whole House will joint me to pray for the missing 
persons and mourn the death of those  who were killed in this worst

The sanitation coverage in the rural areas of the country has 
been only 20% at the beginning of the 10th Plan. Government of 
India have been promoting the sanitation coverage on a campaign 
mode to ensure better health and quality of life for people in the rural 
areas. Government of India have approved an incentive scheme for 
fully sanitized and open defecation free Gram Panchayats, Blocks 
and Districts.

sanitation coverage in terms of (a) 100% sanitation coverage of 
individual house holds, (b) 100% school sanitation coverage 
(c) free from open defecation and (d) clean environment 
maintenance.

for effecting full sanitation coverage in the respective geographical 
area.

case.

discretion of the court and subject to the provisions of the Indian 
Evidence Act, 1872, be treated as evidence.

Discussion with J & K  Government 
2461. SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD : Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether he had convened a meeting in 31st March, 2003 with 
the Jammu and Kashmir Government to discuss various issues; 
(b) if so, whether this included security scenario and implications of 
the various policies of the State Government in the wake of Nadimarg 
massacre; and 
(c) if so, the broad features thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. High Level Meeting had been 
convened under the Chairmanship of Deputy Prime Minister on 
March 31, 2003. 
The meeting considered assessment of the security situation in 
J&K and likely terrorism-related trends in the near future. Steps to be 
taken to counter terrorism were also discussed in detail and it was agreed 
that the Union and State Government would continue to function in complete 
harmony and coordination on all security-related matters pertaining to 
J & K. It was also decided to cons titute a Special Group, pursuant to 
the decision taken in the Meeting, under the Chairmanship of Special 
Secretary (J&K), MHA to review existing macro-strategies of the 
Security Forces and intelligence agencies in J&K and to suggest 
appropriate strategies to be followed to counter terrorism in J&K. 
The Group, which included representatives from army, Government 
of J&K, Central Para Military Forces, intelligence agencies and MHA,

needs amendments so as to provide mode of appointment of Inquiry 
Commission and its terms of reference to inspire confidence in its 
independence and make its findings and recommendations public;

and 
(c) if the answer to parts (a) and (b) be negative, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMl): (a) Section 3(1) of the Commissions of inquiry Act, 
80 

[13 August, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
1952 provides that the appropriate Government may, if it is of opinion 
that it is necessary so to do, and shall, if a resolution in this behalf is 
passed by each House of Parliame nt or, as the case may be, the 
Legislature of the State, by notificati on in the Official Gazette, appoint a 
Commission of Inquiry for the purpose of making an inquiry into any 
definite matter of public importance and performing such functions and 
within such time as may be specified in the notification, and the 
Commission so appointed shall make the inquiry and perform the 
functions accordingly. 
Section 3(4) of the Act provides that the appropriate Government 
shall cause to be laid before each House of Parliament or, as the case 
may be, the Legislature of the State, the report, if any, of the Commission 
on the inquiry made by the Commission under sub-section (1) together 
with a memorandum of the action taken thereon, within a period of six 
months of the submission of the report by the Commission to the 
appropriate Government. 
Since sufficient provisions already exist in the Act regarding mode of 
appointment of Inquiry Commission, its terms of reference, make its 
findings and recommendations public and inspire confidence in its 
indepenence, there is no proposal to amend the Commissions of Inquiry 
Act, 1952.

Supply of drinking water in rural areas 
2498. SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: 
                 DR.T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have approved an additional Rs. 700 Crore 
for three schemes for improving supply of drinking water in rural India; 
(b) if so, what are the three schemes for which this amount has been 
sanctioned; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
139 

RAJYA SABHA [13 August, 2003] 
(c) whetherr the amount sanctioned is sufficient for completing those 
projects; 
(d) whether according to the study conducted by Government, the 
main areas of concern in the rural water supply sector was coverage of 
habitations including schools in the rural areas and ensuring sustainability 
of systems and sourrces; and 
(e) if so, what are the steps suggested by them in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ANNASAHEB M.K. PATIL): (a) to (c) Yes Sir, 
Rs. 700 Crore have been approved for three programmes viz. 
(i) Installation of 1 -lakh-hand pumps, (ii) revival of 1 -lakh traditional sources 
of water and (iii) providing drinking water facility in 1-lakh rural primary 
schools. The total cost for implementation of these programme is Rs. 
800 Crores. Rs. 80 Crores (10%) will be the community participation and 
Rs. 20 crores will be utilised from the existing provisions. 
(d) and (e) Coverage of habitations and ensuring sustainability of systems 
and sources are the main areas of concern in the Rural Water Supply 
Sector. Experience has shown that supply driven non-participatory approach 
has led to the failure of some water supply systems and sources. It was 
felt that participatory demand driven approach will ensure sustainbility. With 
this aim reforms were initiated in 1999 in 67 sector Reform Pilot Project. 
The reform initiatives have now been scaled up to cover the entire country 
by launching the swajaldhara programme on 25th December, 2002.

Study Conducted by the Textile Committee 
2539. SHRIMATI N.R DURGA : Will the Minister of TEXTILES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that accord ing to a study conducted by the 
Textile Committee to.assess the impact of reforms on the functioning of 
the Committee said that reforms su cceeded in changing the Committee 
from abominable regulations to growth-led facilitation; and 
(b) what are the other major outcome of study conducted by the 
Textile Committee? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES 
(SHRI BASAN GOUDA R. PATIL): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir.The major outcome 
of the study conducted by the Textiles Committee are as under:— 
1. The Textiles Committee, which used to be primarily an 
Inspection Agency till early 1990s, has oriented itself to 
become a facilitator in assisting the textile industry, in quality 
improvement in the wake of withdrawal of compulsory pre- 
export inspections under economic liberalization process. 
2. The objective of the Quality Assurance which was sought to 
be achieved through "inspections" earlier is being achieved 
through "facilitation" in the form of Total Quality Management 
(TQM) consultancy, testing services, Human Resource 
Development (HRD) etc. 
3. The performance of several programmes/activities of the 
Committee such as Testing services, TQM Consultancy and 
Market Research has increased considerably in terms of 
diversity, utility, increased us ers and acceptability in the 
industry. 
4. The organization has been continuously improving and 
innovating its activities to match the industry's expectations. 
5. The internal revenue generated by the Committee through 
user charges has increased significantly, by putting the 
organization in the path of achieving financial self- 
sustainability in near future. 
6. The transformation and its management that took place in 
Textiles Committee has relevance and replicability to other

institutions in developing economies like India where the 
support service institutions are to be deregulated and to be

Accreditation of technical and educational institutions 
*289. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that as per the report of the Comptroller and 
Auditor General (CAG) on the state of our Technical and Educational 
Institutions, none of the 171 Institutes audited by them could fulfil the  
AICTE requirements necessary for accreditation; and 
(b) if so, what are the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. 
MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) and (b) As per Section 10 (k) of the 
AICTE Act, 1987, AICTE grants approval for starting new technical 
institutions and introducting new courses/increasing intake following a 
prescribed procedure. Accreditation of programmes is different from 
approval process. It is a process of quality assurance. AICTE has set 
up the National Board of Accreditation (NBA) in terms of Section 10(u) 
of the Act. The 171 Institutions test-checked in audit and mentioned in 
the Report of the Comptroller & Aud itor General of India (C&AG) were 
accorded approval by AICTE during the period 1997 -98 to 2001-02. 
As per the NBA guidelines, the minimum eligibility criteria for a 
programme to be considered for accreditation is that, at least two 
batches must have passed out from the concerned programme. As 
such, most of the institutions that were established during the period 
of report i.e. 1997-98 to 2001-02 were not eligible for accreditation. 
The response for accreditation in th e earlier years was poor due to 
lack of understanding and appreciation of the process involved. In 
order to encourage the institutions for getting their programmes 
accredited, AICTE has so far con ducted 49 awareness workshops 
and 14 training workshops.

Reducing Edible Oil Imports 
2078. SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether edible oil imports are projected to hit well over the 41 
per cent mark which reached in 2001 -2002; 
(b) whether edible oil imports is likely to rise more than the last year; 
(c) if so, the total edible oil imports made during the last year; 
(d) to what extent it will be more during the current year; 
(e) whether the Ministry had opposed to reduction of duty on imported 
palm oil and palmolein by the Finance Ministry; and 
(f) by when the efforts would be made to see that the production of 
edible oil in the country is improved, so that imports are reduced? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (d) The import of edible 
oils during 2001-02 was 43.2 lakh metric tonnes and during 2002-03, 
about 42.66 lakh metric tonnes. There are no restriction on import other 
than the applicable rate of custom  duty. The gap between the domestic 
demand and domestic production of edible oils is met by imports. Thus, 
the quantum of import shall depend on domestic demand, domestic 
production and international prices of edible oils. 
(e) Yes, Sir. 
(f) The Government had set up a Technology Mission on Oilseeds 
in 1986 to increase the production and productivity of oilseeds and to 
reduce the import of edible oils. The Mission has launched a Centrally 
Sponsored Oilseeds Production Programme (OPP) in the country. 
Under the scheme financial assistance is provided on various inputs 
like production and distribution of seeds, distribution of seed minikits, 
distribution of improved farm implements, sprinkler sets, rhyzobium 
culture and micro nutrients etc. In order to disseminate the production 
technology amongst the farmers frontline demonstrations are organized 
by the I.C.A.R. and block demonstrations are organized by the State 
Deptt. of Agriculture. 
218 

[13 August, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
In case the weather conditions remain favourable during the coming 
years, the production of oilseeds is likely to increase from the present 
level which will reduce import of edible oils.

hazardous' to health and banned in many countries;

Production and procurement of potatoes 
†2086. SHRI LAJPAT RAI: 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that production of potatoes is continuously 
increasing in the country for last decade; 
(b) if so, whether it is also a fact that alongwith the increase in the 
production of potatoes, its cost of production is also increasing; 
(c) if so, the facts in this regard; and 
(d) whether it is also a fact that due to non-availability of proper 
arrangement for marketing of potato es, the potato growers are facing 
financial crises? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) Yes, Sir. The potato 
production in the country has increased from 16.38 Million Tonnes during 
1991 -92 to 24.08 Million Tonnes in the year 2001 -02. 
(b) and (c) Yes, Sir. The cost of production is increasing with increase 
in cost of inputs, labour and also with adoption of improved technologies 
of production. As per estimates of Indian Council of Agriculture Research 
cost of production of table potato has increased from Rs. 105/ quintal 
during 2000-01 to Rs. 150/ quintal during 2001-02. 
(d) No, Sir. In order to provide remunerative prices to the farmers, 
the Government of India, on the request of States concerned, provide 
financial assistance through Market Intervention Scheme. During 2002- 
03 the Market Intervention scheme has been implemented in the States 
of Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal where, under the scheme, potato 
has been procured from farmers @ Rs. 190/quintal and Rs. 200/quintal 
respectively. 
Besides, with a view to create new outlets for utilizing the surplus

Post production loss in agriculture sector 
†2087. SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: Will th e Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that 25 percent of post production crop is 
assessed to be lost in agriculture sector of the country; 
(b) if not, facts in this regard; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that su ch loss could be minimized with 
the use of advanced technology; and 
(d) if so, facts in this regard an d how it compares with loss in 
agriculture sector at international level? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b) A Committee headed 
by Dr. V.G. Panse, in its report submitted in 1968, had estimated annual 
post harvest losses in the foodgrains in various stages at 9.33%.These 
included losses during threshing (1.68%), transportation (0.15%), 
processing (0.92%), rodents (2.50%), birds (0.85), insects (2.55%) and 
moisture (0.68%). A survey conducted by Directorate of Marketing and 
inspection, during 1973-74, had estimated post harvest losses in 
foodgrains to be about 5% out of which the storages losses were 
estimated at about 2.7%. A Joint survey conducted by the Indian 
Agricultural Statistics Research Institute and Indian Grain Storage 
Management and Research Institute during 1985—88 in Bulandshahar 
district of Uttar Pradesh and estimated total foodgrains losses at about 
4.12% due to different factors at various post harvest stages. A loss during 
storage and transit of foodgrains in the organized sector is however, less than 
0.5% and 1.5% respectively. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
227 

RAJYA SABHA [13 August, 2003] 
The high level Committee on Cold Storage and Storage constituted 
by Department of Agriculture & Cooperation under the Chairmanship of 
Shri JNL Srivastava, Additional Secretary, in its Report of February 
1999 has estimated 25% to 30% post-harvest losses in horticultural 
produce depending upon the produce, season and the length of journey. 
(c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) In order to reduce losses to food-grains during the post harvest 
period, the Government of India had launched the Save Grain Campaign 
in 1969-70. The main thrust of activ ities of this Scheme is training, 
demonstration and publicity in the field of scientific storage of foodgrains 
at the farm level. Improvement of grain storage structure and 
popularization of scientific storage structures like metal bins, pucca 
kothis and RCC ring bins and other activities are carried out by the 
Save Grain Campaign for the benefit of farmers. 
Foodgrains stocks at commercial level are stored by various 
agencies on scientific lines duri ng which necessary prophylactic and 
curative measures are undertaken to reduce losses. 
In order to promote scientific storage facilites in rural areas and to 
prevent quantitative and qualitative loss es of the produce of the farmers, 
a Central Sector Scheme of construction/renovation of Rural Godowns 
titled "Grameen Bhandaran Yojana" is  being implemented in the country 
since 2001-2002. Under the Scheme, Central Government is providing 
investment subsidy to individual farmers, Self Help Group (SHG), 
Cooperatives, Corporations, Agricultural Produce Marketing Committees 
etc. Subsidy is provided @25% of the capital cost of  the project not 
exceeding Rs. 50.00 lakh for each st orage project through National Bank 
for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) and National 
Cooperative Development Corporation (NCDC). A higher subsidy of 
33.3% of capital cost not exceeding Rs. 60.00 lakhs is  providing for 
beneficiaries belonging to SC/ST and for North-Eastern States and hilly 
areas. So far under the scheme, NABARD has sanctioned 995 projects 
with a capacity of 59.29 lakh tonnes. In addition, 1575 projects with a 
capacity of 7.42 lakh tonnes have been sanctioned by NCDC for 
construction of new rural godowns. 
A Capital investment Subsidy Scheme for construction of cold 
storage  is being  implemented by National Horticulture Board (NHB) 
228 

[13 August, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
through NABARD and NCDC to en hance the storage capacity for 
perishable commodities. Under the scheme, back-ended capital 
investment subsidy is provided to the eligible organisation @ 25% of 
the project cost not exceeding Rs. 50.00 lakh per project and @ 33.33% 
of the project cost upto a ceiling Rs. 60.00 lakh per project for North 
Eastern States. The Board has, so far, approved assistance of 
Rs. 208.17 crore under the scheme for creation of additional storage 
capacity of 31.79 lakh tonnes. 
No study has been conducted to compare post harvest losses in 
India with other countries.

drought, earthquake, fire, flood and hailstorm. 
As per the scheme of National Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF), 
which is based on the recommendations of the EFC, financial assistance 
from NCCF is considered in the wa ke of a calamity of severe nature, 
taking into account the funds required  for relief according to the norms 
laid down, and the funds available in CRF of the State Government, to 
which Government of India contributes 75%. 
The CRF allocation to Himachal Pradesh for the year 2003-04 is 
Rs. 50.33 crore, out of which the Ce ntral share is Rs. 37.75 crore. The 
first installment of Central share of Rs. 18.875 crore, due for release on 
1st May, 2003, has been released to the State Government by the Ministry 
of Finance for want of Utilisation Certificate. The entire Central share 
was released to the State for the years 2000-01 to 2002-03. For drought 
of 2002-03, financial assistance of Rs. 14.35 crores from NCCF and 
0.10 Lakh MTs of foodgrains for relief employment were provided to the 
State. 
Government of Himachal Pradesh has not so far submitted any 
memorandum during current financial year for financial assistance from 
NCCF.

Growth of agriculture sector 
2101. SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any meaningful growth in the agriculture sector is 
expected in 2003-04, if so, what is the basis therefor; and 
(b) whether Central and State Government are contemplating fresh 
investments in the irrigation facilities to bring additional areas under 
agriculture and whether Government is considering crop diversification 
so as to make agriculture more remunerative for farmers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) The favourable monsoon 
rainfall has boosted the prospects of higher growth in the agriculture sector 
in 2003-04. The rainfall in the country as a whole in July 2003, which is 
agriculturally very active, was 107% of the Long Period Average (LPA). 
The cumulative rainfall during the period from 1st June to 30th July 2003 
was excess/normal in 32 out of 36 meteorological sub-divisions. 
244 

[13 August, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(b) As irrigation is a State subject , all types of projects for creating 
Irrigation facilities are conceived, planned and implemented by the State 
Governments through the State sector plan investments according to 
the priority of the respective State Governments. The Planning 
Commission has approved an outlay of Rs. 92,144 crore in the Tenth 
Plan for Irrigation and Flood Control under State Plan. In addition to the 
State Plan allocation, Union Government is providing Central Loan 
Assistance (CLA) to the States under the Accelerated Irrigation Benefits 
Programme (AIBP) since 1996-97 for expeditious completion of on-going 
Irrigation Projects. An amount of Rs. 11,542 crore has been released 
upto March, 2003 as CLA to the States under AIBP. 
The basic aim of crop diversifi cation is to protect the natural 
resources viz soil health and to avoid over exploitation of ground water. 
Accordingly, the States are being advised to increase area under pulses 
and oilseeds crops. The Central Government has been announcing 
relatively higher Minimum Support Prices for pulses and oilseeds with a 
view to making crop diversification more remunerative for the farmers.

Increase in bird trade 
2120. PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that bird trade is on the increase; and 
(b) if so, what measures Government propose to take to check this 
menace? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI DILIP SINGH JUDEV): (a) and (b) The Wild Life 
(Protection) Act, 1972 prohibits trade in rare and endangered species of 
birds and regulates trade in other species of birds. Prevention and 
regulation of trade in birds is the responsibility of State Governments 
and there are no confirmed reports regarding increase in trade of birds. 
Government has, however, taken several measures in this regard.These 
are as follows: 
(i) Rare and endangered species of birds are included in the 
Schedule-I of Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972. Hunting of birds, 
disturbing or damaging their eggs or nests is a punishable offence. 
(ii) Trade in species of birds included in Schedule-IV is permitted 
with licence. Transportation of such birds is also regulated and 
no person can purchase, receive or acquire birds from a person 
not authorized to sale. 
(iii) Export of birds included in the Schedules of the Wild Life 
(Protection) Act, 1972 is prohib ited. Only six species of exotic 
birds are permitted for export. 
(iv) Government of India has set up Regional and Sub-regional offices 
for wild life preservation in major export and trade centres of the 
country to prevent smuggling of birds, wild animals and their 
products. 
(v) Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has been empowered under 
the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 to apprehend and prosecute 
269 

RAJYA SABHA [13 August, 2003] 
wild life offenders. Anti-poaching efforts are being coordinated with 
INTERPOL. 
(vi) Government of India seeks international co-operation under the 
provisions of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered 
Species of Wild Flora and Fauna (CITES) for control of illegal 
trade in wild life items.

Saving Kaziranga Sanctuary from flood 
2123. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHAR JEE: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Kaziranga, the abode of the world famous, 
one horned rhinoceros is on the verge of collapse at the height of flood 
waves; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) whether Government are aware that the ravage by the floods 
has become an annual feature which destroys wildlife of the sanctuary 
regularly and if so, the short-term and long-term measures proposed to 
be taken to save the sanctuary from the flood waters causing havoc 
every year?f 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI DILIP SINGH JUDEV): 
(a) No, Sir. 
(b) Does not arise. 
(c) Annual flood is a natural phenomenon for a riverine ecosystem 
like Kaziranga National Park (KNP). However, at the time of high flood. 
278 

[13 August, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
which occurs in the park over a cycle of 7-8 years, some damage to 
both infrastructure and wildlife take s place. Various short-term and long- 
term measures taken to save the wildlife at KNP include: 
1. Dovetailing the efforts of the Government, Non-government 
Organisations and public for watch and ward and rescue of animals. 
2. Intensifying patrolling in vulnerable areas and establishing 
temporary camps wherever necessary. 
3. Regulating speed of vehicles by erecting barriers on National 
Highway (NH) 37 and round-the-clock monitoring the movement of 
animals crossing the NH-37. 
4. Pressing into service Mobile Animal Rescue Van. 
5. Periodic desiltation of water bodies. 
6. Construction of artificial highlands in the park.

Adverse impact on environment and health due to pollution 
2125. SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government agree that phenomenal growth of industries 
in non-conforming areas in Delhi has le d to a severe adverse impact on 
the environment of Delhi and health of the residents; 
(b) if so, whether air pollution is responsible for the emergency 
hospitalisation of patients with breathing and heart problems; and 
(c) if so, what steps Government have taken or are taking to save 
people from adverse impact of pollution? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI DILIP SINGH JUDEV): (a) and (b) According 
to the Central Pollution Control Board, the ambient levels of Sulfur Dioxide

formulation of Comprehensive Policy for Abatement of Pollution, supply

management of municipal & bio-medical wastes, promotion of cleaner

preparation and implementation of action plans for major cities & critically 
polluted areas.

Objectives of National and State Women's Commissions 
[Extracts of section 10(1) of National Commission for Women Act, 
1990 on functions of National Commission for Women] 
10. Function of the Commission .—(1) The Commission shall 
perform all or any of the following functions, namely:— 
(a) investigate and examine all matters relating to the safeguards 
provided for women under the Constitution and other laws; 
(b) present to the Central Government, annually and at such other 
times as the Commission may deem fit, reports upon the working 
of those safeguards; 
301 

RAJYA  SABHA [13 August, 2003] 
(c) make in such reports recomm endations for the effective 
implementation of those safeguards for improving the conditions 
of women by the Union or any State; 
(d) review, from time to time, the existing provisions of the Constitution 
and other laws affecting women and recommend amendments 
thereto so as to suggest remedial legislative measures to meet 
any lacunae, inadequacies or shortcomings in such legislations; 
(e) take up the cases of violation of the provisions of the Constitution 
and of other laws relating to women with the appropriate 
authorities; 
(f) look into complaints and take suo moto notice of matters relating 
to— 
(i) deprivation of women's rights; 
(ii) non-implementation of laws  enacted to provide protection 
to women and also to achieve the objective of equality and 
development. 
(iii) non-compliance of policy decisions, guidelines or 
instructions aimed at mitigating hardships and ensuring 
welfare and providing relief to women and take up the 
issues arising out of such matters with appropriate 
authorities; 
(g) call for special studies or inves tigations into specific problems or 
situations arising out of discrimination and atrocities against 
women and identify the constraints so as to recommend strategies 
for their removal; 
(h) undertake promotional and educational research so as to suggest 
ways of ensuring due representation of women in all spheres 
and identify factors responsible for impending their advancement, 
such as, lack of access to housin g and basic services, inadequate 
support services and technologies for reducing drudgery and 
occupational health hazards and for increasing their productivity; 
(i) participate and advise on the planning process of socio-economic 
development of women; 
302 

[13 August, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(j) evaluate the progress of the development of women under the 
Union and any State; 
(k) inspect or cause to be inspected a jail, remand home, women's 
institution or other place of cust ody where women are kept as 
prisoners or otherwise, and take up with the concerned authorities 
for remedial action, if found necessary; 
(I) fund litigation involving issues affecting a large body of women; 
(m) make periodical reports to  the Government on any matter 
pertaining to women and in particular various difficulties under 
which women toil; 
(n) any other matter which may be referred to it by the Central 
Government.

(SHRI BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a) an d (b) Various safety hazards in

are provided with ballast-less track to take care of track maintenance

the passage of the water with cover on the top to act as pathway and 
refuges have been provided in the tunnels for men and trolley to 
accomodate themselves when the train is passing. Communication 
sockets are provided at 400 m in  tunnels to ensu re communication 
between the train crew and the contro l office in case of any emergency.

(b) why does Railways allow tea/ coffee vendors to carry burning 
stoves/chulahs in the compartments; and 
(c) why there is no fire extinguishers existed in all compartments in 
Indian Railway even after many incidents of fire reported in the past? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a) Indi an Railways are continuously 
upgrading the fire retardant properties of each and every material used in 
coach construction so that the coach can sustain prolonged  priods of 
exposure to fire caused in-adverten tly from external sources such as 
inflammable material in the luggage of passengers etc.

[13 August, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
Some of the important specific measures that have been taken over  
the years in this direction are:— 
* Switching over from a wooden body coach to an all metal 
construction.

and fire fighting sta ndards (UIC-564II) and IS specifications for 
flammability and fire retardance properties of various material 
utilized in manufacture of Indian Railway Coaches. 
* Adoption of naval Specification (NCD 1409,1410 and 1411) and 
FAR (Airline Safety) specification for toxicity and smoke level 
emission for upholstery, fabric and curtains. 
Notices are also displayed prominently in all coaches prohibiting 
passengers from carrying any inflammable or explosive materials.

strictly prohibited in station premises/trains as per provisions of law and 
no person carrying such articles is allowed. Regular checks and drives 
are conducted by the Railway staff in trains against those persons who 
carry inflammable and prohibited articles unauthorizedly, and action is 
taken against them as provided in law.

are continuously manned by Railway personnel, such as train engine, 
guard compartment, pantry car and air-conditioned coaches. Fire 
extinguishers are not provided in other unmanned coaches as safe 
keeping of these costly items cannot be ensured.

Steel exports to China 
2223. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: 
Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that China opened its doors for importing 
Steel from India and Other countries of the world; 
(b) if so, whether Beijing has issued any import quota for us; 
(c) if so, for how long this quota system is valid; 
(d) the total potential of steel India can export to China before quota 
system closes; and 
(e) how Government are planning to grab the opportunity of exporting 
steel to China? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF STEEL 
(SHRI BRAJ KISHORE TRIPATHY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) In May 2002, China initiated safeguard investigations 
against import of various categories of steel from several countries, 
including India. In November 2002 the investigations were completed 
361 

RAJYA SABHA [13 August, 2003] 
and final safeguard measures in the form of quotas on five categories 
of steel items were imposed with additional tariff in case the imports 
exceed the relevant quota. These m easures would be in place for the 
next two and a half years. However, these measures do not apply to 
India. 
(d) In accordance with the WTO ru les China has exempted the 
developing countries, including India from the safeguard measures. 
However, the exemption is subject to the condition that import share of 
a developing country in a particular category should not exceed 3% of 
China's total import volume in that category. 
(e) A delegation led by the Minister of State for Steel visited China 
from May 18-23, 2002. The purpose of the visit was to explore 
opportunities of cooperation in the Iron and Steel sector. At times, the 
public sector undertakings under the Ministry of Steel and delegations 
to China to promote exports, source raw materials and explore areas of 
co-operation. Apart from these Ministry and PSU initiatives, the Embassy 
of India, Beijing has also identified products which are in demand under 
the Harmonised System Code 72 (Iron and Steel) in the Chinese market 
and the necessary information has been forwarded to the concerned 
Indian Chambers of Commerce/Export  Councils and industry players 
active in the field of Iron and Steel. The Indian Steel Alliance, working 
under the aegis of the confederation of India Industry (Cll), has already 
initiated talks with the Chinese government and steel companies in China 
to increase trade between the two countries. 
The Ministry is thus actively involved in various promotional efforts 
in consultation with the industry and their Associations. The Government 
is fully discharging its role as a facilitator in a liberalised environment 
and helping the industry to adequately exploit the market potential.

*310.  SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: 
SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN: 
Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Supreme Court of India has underlined the need for

country;

THE MINISTER OF LAW  AND JUSTICE (SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): 
(a) and (b) The Supreme Court of India in its judgement delivered on 
384 

[13 August, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
21.7.2003 in the matter of John Vallamattom Vs Union of India has made 
certain observations in respect of the need for enactment of a Uniform 
Civil Code. The relevant extracts fr om the judgement are annexed as 
Statement. (See below). 
(c) There is no decision taken by the Government to frame a Uniform 
Civil Code. 
Statement 
Relevant extracts from the judgement delierved by the 
Supreme Court of India 
The Supreme Court of India in its judgement delivered on 21.7.2003 
in th matter of John Vallamattom Vs Union of India has observed in para 
44 of the said judgement as under:- 
"44. Before I part with the case I would like to state that article 44 
provides that the State shall end eavour to secure for the citizens a 
Uniform Civil Code throughtout the territory of India. The  aforesaid 
provision is based on the premise that there is no necessary 
connection between religious and personal law in a civilized society. 
Article 25 of the Constitution confers freedom of conscience and 
fee profession, practice and propagation of the religion.The aforesaid 
two provisions viz. articles 25 and 44 show that the former guarantees 
religious freedom whereas the latter divests religion from social 
relations and personal law. It is no matter of doubt that marriage, 
succession and the like matters of a secular character cannot be 
brought within the guarantee enshrined under articles 25 and 26 of 
the Constitution. Any legislation which bring succession and the 
like matters of secular character within the ambit of articles 25 & 26 
is a suspect legislation. Although it is doubtful whether the American 
doctrine of suspect legislation is followed in this country. In 
Smt. Sarla Mudgal, President, Kalyani and others Vs Union of India 
and others (1995 (3) SGC 635), it was held that marriage, sucession 
and like matters of secu lar character cannot be brought within the 
guarantee enshrined under articles 25 & 26 of the Constitution. It is 
a matter of regret that article 44 of the Constitution has not been 
given effect to. Parliament is still to step in for framing a common 
civil code in the country. A common civil code will help the cause of 
385 

RAJYA  SABHA [13 August, 2003] 
national integration by removi ng the contradictions based on 
ideologies".

*311. SHRI EKANATH K.  THAKUR: Will the Minister of HEALTH

in the world, only 55 per cent Indians were covered by DOTS in 2002;

50% are sputum positive, which are infectious cases of TB. However, 
the incidence of TB in India estima ted by WHO at 178 cases per lakh 
population is lower than the rate of incidence in many high ranking 
countries but due to the large population size in India the actual number 
of patients in the country is larger. 
DOTS coverage is being rapidly expanded in the country. From

covered at present. It is envisaged to cover 850 million population by

*315. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND

(SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) to (c) Government of India, through 
NACO, is implementing a comprehensive National AIDS Control 
Programme across the country through State AIDS Control Societies. 
The World Health Organization (WHO) , in their Global Programme on 
AIDS (GPA), popularized the ABC approach which is being followed in 
over 150 countries, and is by now,  an internationally accepted media 
and program strategy. It is based on the belief that HIV is a problem 
with a solution. It contemplates bringing about behaviour change within 
high risk behaviours that include, but are not limited to: 
Abstinence and/or delayed sexual debut; 
390 

[13 August, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
Being faithful to, and developing fidelity towards single partner 
relationships; and

immense potential for exports, including under the General Agreement

Trade in Services (CTS) of the WT O with the objective of bringing 
about deeper liberalisation and removal of barriers being faced by 
our IT professionals and service providers. Our keen interest in the 
Information Technology se ctor in providing more access for our service 
providers and IT professionals in markets abroad and the advantages 
that would accrue to othe r countries throu gh liberalisation of this sector
