Export of commercial services 
2262. SHRI R.S. GAV AI: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) the present status so far India's exports of commercial services 
is concerned; and 
(b) the details of the measures taken by Government to increase 
export of commercial services? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) As per the 
latest WTO report, the value of exports of commercial services made by 
India in 2002 is placed at US$ 20.7 billion constituting 1.3% of the world 
exports of commercial services. The rate of growth of export of 
commercial services in 2002 over the previous year was 8% in dollar 
terms. 
(b) Under the Exim Policy, the Government has formulated a scheme 
wherein Service Providers have been allowed duty free credit entitlement 
for import of spares, office equipment and furniture, professional equipment 
and consumables, except the agriculture and dairy products. The en titlement 
would be equivalent to 10% of the average foreign exchange earned by them 
in the preceding three licensing years excepting for the Service Providers in the 
Tourism Sector. The entitlement in the case of hotels of the category of three 
star and above and those related to the Tourism Sector, registered with the 
Department of Tourism, 
428 

[13 August, 2003] RAJYA    SABHA 
would be 5% of the average foreig n exchange earned by them in the 
preceding three licensing years. The scheme will cover only those Service 
Providers who have an average fo reign exchange earning of over 
Rs. 10 lakhs in the preceding three licensing years. 
Border trade through N.E. Corridor 
2263. DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) the clause-wise implementation st atus of the package finalized 
towards upgradation of trade and commerce with the neighbouring countries 
through N.E. corridor showing location-wise infrastructure developed so far 
and the achievements made: 
(b) the details of the agreements reached with the neighbouring  ountries 
for promotion of border trade: and 
(c) the progress made on reopening and improvement of Stillwell road, 
connecting N.H. 38 through Myanmar? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) onsequent 
to the visit of the Hon'ble Prime Minister, the Central Government has 
set up an Empowered Committee on Promotion of Trade and Exports in 
North East and Sikkim.The important steps taken to upgrade trade and 
commerce with the neighbouring countries through the North East region 
are as under: 
(i) Four border townships at Zokhawtha (Mizoram). Moreh (Manipur). 
Dawki (Meghalaya) and Sutarkhandi (Assam) have been identified 
for development of trade related infrastructure and an amount of 
Rs. 16.29 crores has been sanctioned. 
(ii) A trade-cum-exhibition centre has been sanctioned at Guwahati 
for which an amount of Rs. 13.40 crores has been sanctioned. 
(iii) 'APEDA has sanctione d four reefer vans in the North East region 
for perishable goods and has set up a cold storage at Guwahati. 
(iv)  An Agri Export Zone has been sanctioned in Assam. 
429 

RAJYA  SABHA [13 August, 2003] 
(v) Under the Export Development Fund scheme Rs. 9.30 crores 
has been sanctioned for promotion of exports from the North East 
region. Some of the important projects sanctioned include Pilot 
project for handloom exports from Nagaland & Arunachal Pradesh. 
Project for international marketing of North Eastern handicrafts, 
Project for exports of orchids from Sikkim, 100% Export oriented 
unit for Hydro-Carbon Free yarn project. 
(vi) Development of Land Custom Stations in the North East has 
also been taken up. 
(b) India has border trade agreem ents with Myanmar and China. 
India has signed a border trade ag reement with Myanmar on 21.1.94. 
The agreement provide for border trade initially through Moreh (Manipur) 
and Champhai (Mizoram) and subsequently through any other point to 
be mutually identified. Currently, border trade with Myanmar is being 
conducted through Moreh only. Recently, India and China have agreed 
to use Nathula as the Pass for entr y and exit of persons, means and 
transport and commodities engaged in border trade.

(b) whether Government have thought of any remedial action; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c) Leptospirosis is prevalent 
in Gujarat, Maharashtra, Kerala , Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and A&N. 
Islands. Cases of Leptospirosis have been reported from Shimoga district 
of Karnataka since 2002. Following measures are taken by Government 
of India through National Institute of Communicable Diseases (NICD), 
Delhi covering all parts of the country including the State of Karnataka:- 
1. Physicians have been sensitized in affected States. 
2. The NICD has the diagnostic facilities for the diagnosis of 
Leptospirosis. It provides diagnostic support for the same to 
various institutions. 
3. NICD provides investigative suppor t to outbreak of leptospirosis 
in any part of the country wherever asked/required to do so. 
4. To create awareness about the dis ease, an issue of 'CD-Alert' 
covering aspects of leptospirosis including prevention and control 
is circulated to all the concerned health authorities in different 
States and Union Territories. 
5. National Surveillance Programme for Communicable Diseases 
is being implemented in 101 districts of the country. Surveillance 
of leptospirosis is one of the diseases covered in this 
programme.

SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: 
SHRI JHUMUK LAL BHENDIA:

State came in late;

by IICD? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) While control of outbreaks of 
any disease is the responsibility of the respective State Governments, 
Government of India provides technical support to the States by sending 
expert teams to the affected stat es for guidance. During the recent 
outbreak of viral encephalitis in Andhra Pradesh, support has also been 
provided for laboratory confirmation for diagnosis of the outbreaks. In 
addition to the insecticides and larv icides already provided under the 
National Anti Malaria Programme, arrangements have been made for 
additional supply of Maiathion (Technical) for fogging and larvicides for

306 cases and 168 deaths due to viral encephalitis during 2003 in Andhra

2003 for investigation and technical support immediately after the 
news of outbreak was reported and held discussions with the State 
Health Authorities. 
The Central Teams from the National Institute of Communicable 
Diseases (NICD), New Delh i and the National Institute of Virology (NIV), 
Pune also visited the outbreak a ffected areas. Laboratory reports 
from NICD and NIV indicate that the outbreaks in Andhra Pradesh is 
due to viral encephalitis. The Government of India deputed another team

of contagious diseases are prevalent in the country. A part from various 
steps taken to strengthen the public health system in order to ensure 
early detection and treatment of diseases at the point of first contact, a 
number of focused disease control programmes are being run by the 
Government for identification and control of various diseases like 
Tuberculosis, HIV/AIDS, Leprosy and surveillance of other communicable 
diseases. 
The National Surveillance Progra mme for Communicable Diseases 
was launched as a pilot programme in 1997-98 in 5 districts with a view 
to strengthen the disease surveill ace system of various communicable 
diseases so that early warning signals of outbreaks are recognized and 
appropriate follow-up action is initiated.The programme is implemented 
through the existing health infrastrcture and surveillance system involving 
training of medical and para-medical personnel, upgradation of 
laboratories and improvement in communication system.The programme 
is currently implemented in 101 districts. Under the 10th Five Year Plan, 
a Project Implementation Plan is en visaged to strengthen the existing 
surveillance system at the District, State and National levels. 
The Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP) has been 
in operation in the country since 1952. To achieve a cure rate of 85% of 
new sputum positive cases and to detect at least 70% of such cases, 
Revised National T.B. Control Programme (RNTCP) which is Directly 
Observed Treatment—Short Course (DOTS) Strategy, is implemented 
in the country in a phased manner. Under the Programme, 100% 
requirement of anti-TB drugs and Binocular Microscopes are provided 
as commodity grant by the Centre to all the States/UTs for undertaking 
various activities for implementation of RNTCP, Cash assistance is 
released to States/District TB Societies. The Programme is regorously 
monitored through quarterly performance reports. 
In order to combat the problem of AIDS, Government has launched 
a comprehensive AIDS prevention and control programme, which is a 
100% centrally sponsored scheme implemented in all States/UTs 
through States/UTs' AIDS Control Societies. The main components of 
the Programme consist of:- 
• Reducing the spread of HIV in groups at high risk by identification 
of target population and providing peer counseling, condom 
451 

RAJYA  SABHA [13 August, 2003] 
promotion, and treatment of sexually transmitted infections. 
• Preventive intervention for the general population by Information, 
Education and Communication (IEC) and awareness compaign, 
provision of voluntary testing and counseling, safe blood 
transfusion services and prevention of occupational exposure. 
• Providing financial assistance for opportunistic infections home 
and community based care. 
• Strengthening effectiveness and technical managerial, financial 
sustainability at National, State, and Municipal levels. 
• Promoting collaboration amongst public, private and voluntary 
sector. 
For the elimination of Leprosy in the country, the Government of 
India is implementing National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP), 
a 100% Centrally sponsored Scheme  with the objec tive of achieving 
the elimination of Leprosy, i.e. prevalence of less than 1 case per 10,000 
population at national level by the year 2005.

2291. SHRI SATISH PRADHAN: Will th e Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have constituted a National Health Fund 
to provide medical assistance to the helpless and poor people; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and

all sections of the society get quality health care facility?

FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) On the recommendation of the 
Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human 
Resources Development, a National Illness Assistance Fund was set 
up in 1997. Its name has now been changed as "Rashtriya Arogya 
Nidhi" vide Government's Resolution No. W. 11011/2/2003-NIAF dated

2292. SHRI SHAHID SIDD IQUI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether in the light of a number of patients from foreign countries 
wanting to avail health care facilities in India, Government have 
conducted a survey on further development of these opportunities; 
(b) whether Government have taken any steps to develop Medical 
Tourism which is expected to fetch 10 thousand crore additional revenue 
by the year 2012; and 
457 

RAJYA SABHA [13 August, 2003] 
(c) whether Government are preparing a joint programme with the 
Ministries of Tourism an Civil Aviation to bring more tourists in the health 
sector? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c) The Government is aware 
that certain hospitals in India are offering quality medical care in areas 
such as Cardiac Surgery, Ophthalmol ogy etc. at a fraction of the cost 
incurred in developed countries. A report commissioned by the 
Confederation of Indian Industry in association with M/s Mskinsey has 
outlined the great potential for medical tourism in India due to a strong 
value preposition on cost, quality and services. 
It is the endeavor of the government to provide quality medical care 
to all citizens and also to promote the use of quality facilities for treatment 
of needy patients from other countries. For this purpose, India is one of the 
few countries to have given a commitment for allowing foreign investments 
in the hospital sector with a cap on foreign equity to the extent on 51%.

policy which provides for duty free imports equivalent of 10% of average 
foreign exchange earning in preced ing three years by health service 
providers.

sector both from private and public sources, India's potential in medical 
tourism will continue to expand.

ratio as 407 for the year 1998. Based on this, it is estimated the above.

2299. SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: W ill the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state:

of the World Health Organisation that non-communicable diseases would 
account for over 55 per cent of deaths in India by 2020;

awareness among the public for a dopting the basic life style changes 
as recommended by WHO;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (d) Yes, Sir. As the major 
non-communicable disease like Diab etes, Cardio-Vascular Diseases 
(CVD), Cancer etc. are life style related diseases, it is very important to 
adopt preventive lifestyle interventio n measures such as healthy diet, 
increased physical activity, avoidan ce to tobacco and stress, weight 
reduction etc. These interventio ns are being emphasized through 
information, education & communication (IEC) activities of the 
Government including through Central Health Education Bureau (CHEB).

time in which various Central and State Organizations participate and 
disseminate health awareness messages.

District Cancer Control Programme, the Non-Governmental Organizations 
and the Regional Cancer Centres, Cancer awareness programmes are 
telecast through Kalyani Tele Magazine of Prasar Bharti in 8 States.

2311. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of HEALTH

planning is yet to catch on in slums; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and

476 

[13 August, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) A study was presented 
during the XXth Annual Conference of In dian Society of Medical Statistics 
at Indian Council of Medical Research, New Delhi on 19-22, December, 
2002. The study was based upon a sample survey on the status of 
fertility and family planning in 21 slums out of 218 slums in Varanasi of 
Uttar Pradesh. The study has high lighted the acceptance of family 
planning at higher parity slowing the pace of fertili ty decline. The study 
also mentioned that non-adoption of  spacing methods of contraception, 
early age of marriage and preference  for male child result in higher 
fertility. 
(c) Two National Family Health Surveys carried out in 1992-93 
(NFHS-I) and in 1998-99 (NFHS-II) have shown the overall improvement 
in the status of Contraceptive Prevalence Rate. The Contraceptive 
Prevalence Rate in the country has improved from 40.6% to 48.2% in 
total, from 51.0% to 58.2% in urban areas and from 36.9% to 44.7% in 
rural areas.

THE MINISTER OF STATE FOR LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI P.C. 
THOMAS):, (a) and (b) Allegations of deviant behaviour involving acts of 
corruption and moral turpitude, against some members of Judicial Service 
of the States and some Judges of High Courts have come to the notice of

Constitution, the State Government frames rules and regulations in

officers of District/Sessions Courts, the disciplinary control lies with the 
concerned High Court. Under these circumstances the Central 
Government is not maintaining a data on this.

procedure for the investigation and proof of the misbehaviour or 
incapacity of a Judge of  the Supreme Court or High Court and for the 
presentation of an address by Parliame nt to the President and for matters 
connected therewith. Subordinate Judiciary does not come under the 
purview of this Act. However, the Constitution (Ninety-Eighth 
Amendment) Bill, 2003 propose to vest the power of inquiry into cases 
of misconduct or such deviant behaviour of a Judge, other than those 
calling for his removal, in the National Judicial Commission.The Bill has

Beggars in Delhi 
2362. SHRI RAJU PARMAR: Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of  the fact that begging is an 
organized racket in Delhi; 
(b) if so, the action taken by Government to completely remove 
begging from the inter-sections and other hot spots of NCT of Delhi; 
and 
(c) whether Government have ever  launched a drive to punish 
beggars during the last two years, and if so, the reasons for continuation 
of various gangs of beggars operating in Delhi? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL 
JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRI NAGMANI): (a) to (c) As per 
the information furnished by the Department of Social Welfare, 
Government of NCT of Delhi, there is no authentic report to suggest 
incidence of begging through any organized racket in Delhi. 
Begging is an offence under Section 4 of the Bombay Prevention 
of Begging Act, 1959. Regular anti-begging raids are conducted in 
association with the Delhi Police under the said Act. Special drives and 
anti-begging awareness campaigns are also undertaken from time to 
522 

[13 August, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
time for apprehending beggars at public places and mobilizing public 
opinion against giving alms. After apprehension beggars are produced 
at a special court presided over by a metropolitan magistrate and are 
sent to custodial institutions for beggars where various services are 
provided for weaning them away from beggary and making them self- 
reliant. During th years 2001-02 and 2002-03, 3776 beggars were 
apprehended out of which 1788 beggars were convicted. However, 
there is constant influx of beggars from other States making it difficult 
to completely remove them from public places.

2363. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of SOCIAL 
JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that  there is an increase in the 
number of drug abusers in the country; 
(b) what is the status of such drug abusers; and 
(c) what elaborate steps have been taken by Government to stop 
drug abusers from spreading their ugly tentacles in rural parts of the 
country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL 
JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRI NAGMANI): (a) Various 
surveys and reports indicate an increasing trend of drug abuse amongst 
certain vulnerable sections of the society. 
(b) and (c) While the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance 
is administering Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) 
Act (as amended in the year 2001) for effectively regulating the 
availability of illicit drugs in the country, the Ministry of Social Justice & 
Empowerment is implementing a Scheme entitled "Scheme for 
Prevention of Alcoholism and Substance (Drugs) Abuse" wherein Non- 
Government Organisations are provided with financial support for 
awareness generation, counselling se rvices, treatment and rehabilitation 
of such drugs abusers. In addition,  NGOs are also being funded for 
deaddiction Campus for treatment of addicts in community settings, 
especially in rural ar eas. Around 450 programm es are being funded 
all over the country, including rural areas with an annual allocation of 
Rs. 25.50 crores for treatment and rehabilitation of drug abusers.

concessions) for production of cost-effective building materials 
and import of critical machinery and equipments particularly

RAJYA  SABHA [13 August, 2003] 
Funds to Urban Local Bodies of Uttar Pradesh 
†2377. SHRI MUNAVVAR HASAN: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have taken any steps to strengthen the 
urban local bodies of Uttar Pradesh; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the funds released to the urban local bodies of the State during 
the last three years, year-wise; and 
(d) the results achieved therefrom? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI PON. 
RADHAKRISHNAN): (a) to (d) As per entry 5 of the State List of Seventh 
Schedule of the Constitution, 'local Government' is a State Subject. In 
view of this, it is for the State Government to take necessary steps to 
strengthen urban local bodies. The Ministry of Urban Development & 
Poverty Alleviation have not released any fund to urban local bodies of 
Uttar Pradesh for the purpose of strengthening urban local bodies. 
However, the Government of India have taken a number of steps to 
strengthen urban local bodies (ULBs)  of the country. As the first and 
foremost measure, the Constitution (74th Amendment) Act, 1992 was 
enacted and all the States have amended their Municipal Laws to devolve 
adequate functional and financial powers to municipalities in conformity 
with the provisions enshrined in the above Act. 
States have constituted State Finance Commissions to review the 
financial position of the municipalities and make recommendations to 
the State Government with regard to taxation; sharing of taxes between 
the State Government and Local Gove rnment; principles for governing 
grant-in-aid; and measures for improving the financial position of urban 
local bodies. 
Suitable amendment has also been made to Article 280 of the 
Constitution to make it mandatory that the Central Finance Commission 
shall, inter-alia, make specific recommendations with regard to measures 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
550 

[13 August, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
that are needed to augment the reso urces of a State with a view to 
supplementing the resources of municipalities in the States on the basic 
of the recommendations made by the State Finance Commission. 
Besides, the Govt.of India have initiated needed urban sector reforms 
with a view to strengthening ULBs both in terms of capacity building and 
good financial management. The urban sector reforms include the 
following components: 
• Setting up of Urban Reforms Incentive Fund to provide reform- 
linked assistance to States. 
• Tax-free Municipal Bonds for issue by urban local bodies for 
portable water supply, sewerage of sanitation, drainage, solid 
waste management, roads/bridges/flyovers, and urban transport. 
In addition, the Central Government has announced tax exemption 
in case of bonds issued by municipal/local governments for raising 
resources for urban infrastructure. 
• Urban Development Plans and Implementation Guidelines issued 
in 1996. These guidelines emphasize for innovative approaches 
for fiscal resource mobilization, rationalization of subsidies, 
commercial orientation of urban development plans. 
• Municipal accounting system serves as an effective management 
tool for financial activities of urban local bodies, promote effective 
and timely decision making process and facilitate better 
accountability and transparency. To bring about needed reforms 
in the municipal accounting system, a Task Force was set up to 
suggest accounting and budget formats for urban local bodies. 
The Task Force in its report has recommended for budget and 
accounting formats for ULBs with  appropriate codification and 
classification of budget and acco unt heads. The report of the 
Task Force has been circulated to all States for implementation 
in April, 2003. 
• Government with the objective of simplification and rationalization 
of property tax, which is considered as one of the buoyant sources 
of revenue for urban local bodies, have issued Guidelines to all 
State Governments in 1998. Uttar Pradesh is one of the States 
which is in the process of implementing property tax reforms.

Subletting of Government quarters 
2378. SHRI LAJPAT RAI: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aw are that a large number of 
Government Quarters at Chitra Gupta Road and Aram Bagh have been 
subletted to the contractor's labour by the SDO/JE posted in the area; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the number of raids conducted by Government in this regard 
during the last three years; and 
(d) the action proposed to be taken by Government against the 
officers involved in such activities? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI PON. 
RADHAKRISHNAN): (a) The Directorate of Estates has not received 
any complaint/report regarding subletting of Government quarters at 
Chitra Gupta Road and in Aram Bagh to contractors' labour by the SDO/ 
JE posted in the area. 
(b) Does not arise. 
(c) The number of surprise checks c onducted by the officers of the 
Directorate of Estates during 2000-01, 2001-02 and 2002-03 to detect 
subletting of Government quarters at Chitra Gupta Road and in Aram 
Bagh is 357. 
(d) After following the prescribed procedures under the Allotment 
Rules, the allotment of 108 quarters at Chitra Gupta Road and in Aram 
Bagh has been cancelled on account of subletting by the allottees and 
78 such quarters have been got vacated. 
The allottees of these quarters have also been debarred from further 
allotment for the rest of their service.  Further, the Ministries/Departments 
concerned have been advised to initi ate disciplinary proceedings against 
these Government servants under the applicable Conduct Rules.

Homeless SC & ST families in Urban and Rural Areas 
†2380. SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI : Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of SC and ST families residing in urban areas, rural 
areas and in metropolitan cities as per the data collected by the National 
Building Organisation, which do not have their own houses/ 
accommodation facility; 
(b) out of these, the number of such families in Madhya Pradesh 
and Maharashtra; and 
(c) the steps being taken by Government to provide housing facilities 
to such families? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN  THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI PON 
RADHAKRISHNAN): (a) and (b) National Building Organisation does 
not collect the information on Sc heduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes 
houseless families in rural/urban areas and Metros. 
(c) One of the aims of the National Housing & Habitat Policy 1998 is 
to meet the special needs of Sc heduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes. 
However, since Housing is a State subject it is the responsibility of the 
State Governments to draw up housing schemes for the Scheduled 
Castes/Scheduled Tribes families.

563

†2384. SHRIMATI KUM KUM RAI:  Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have formulated a scheme to construct 
flats at slum land and hand-over the flats to the slum dwellers; 
(b) whether backward States like Biha r have also been included in 
that list;

(d) if not, the reasons therefor?

DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI PON 
RADHAKRISHNAN): (a) to (c) The Government is implementing 0 
centrally sponsored scheme called Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana 
(VAMBAY) to provide shelter or upgrade the existing shelter for people 
living below poverty line in urban slums. The scheme has also a 
component known as Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan (NBA) for the construction 
of community toilets. The scheme is funded with the Government of 
India subsidy of 50% and the balance 50% to be arranged by the State

Government with the ceilling cost prescribed both for dwelling units and 
community toilets. VAMBAY is a demand driven scheme and funds are

the VAMBAY account and submitted proposals, complete in all respects, 
as per the guidelines. An allocation of Rs. 296.68 lakhs during the year 
2001-02, Rs. 1104.37 lakhs during the year 2002-03 and 
Rs. 1044.52 lakhs in the current financial year 2003-04 as Central share 
has been made for the State of Bihar. However, no Central share could

State Government.

grateful to you for giving me this opportunity to offer my views on the 
Science and Technology Policy, 2003,  which was declared by the Prime 
Minister at the 90th session of the Indian  Science Congress, in January, this 
year.    This Policy comes in place of the 1983 Policy, which was, then,

Science Policy was of 1958. New policy became necessary as the Prime 
Minister put it, "because it was necessary to respond to the breath-taking 
changes that have taken place in the world of science and technology in the 
closing decades of the last Century." 
Madam, the amazing achievements of the last Century prompted 
the Time magazine to designate the Centur y not only as the Century of 
Democracy and the Century of Civil Righ ts, but as the Century of Science 
and Technology. Therefore, the perso n of that Century was neither 
Roosevelt nor Gandhi, but was Einstein, who had appropriately said, 
"Politics is for the moment, but an equa tion is for eternity." Therefore, in 
view of the progress of technology duri ng the last Century where, as it is

could think, and particularly, after the advent of internet which started after 
our first Science Policy in 1969, and after the Information Technology 
Revolution of 1990 which really is called the w.w.w. revolution, a new policy 
was highly imperative to meet these new challenges. Madam, normally, 
policies are routinely declared and they form part of the record, but, 
normally, they are not implemented. Personally, I have been involved with 
the field of education for the last 40 ye ars. As we know, the first Education

steps that are being taken for the pur poses of the implem entation of this

for the purposes of understanding t he history of the development of 
science, and probably for the purposes  of understanding several other 
things which are lying in those texts, but which we do not know because of

SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO (Andhra Pradesh): Madam, thank 
you for giving me this opportunity. 
We have emerged as a great country over a period of fifty-six 
years. In this onward progress of our nation, one aspect, which deserves 
mention, is the spectacular advance ment of science and technology. We 
are spending less than one per cent of our GDP on science and technology. 
Compared to many countries of Europe where investments in science and 
technology are two to three per cent of GDP, we, certainly, lag behind. 
Yet, within a limited investment, we have been able to detonate nuclear 
devices, launch our own satellites, plumb the depths of the oceans, 
manufacture our own super computers, at the same time, take care of many 
problems of our country. The success of India as a modern democratic and 
secular Republic is rooted in the success of science and technology. 
600 

[13 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
In fact, I recall that the former President of India, Shri K.R. 
Narayanan, while addressing the nation on the eve of our Independence Day 
in the year 2001, had said, "When demora lisation sets in, think of science in 
India to overcome the demoralisation." This statement is a major indicator 
of the progress registered by our countr y in the highly competitive field of 
science and technology. 
The CSIR wastes crores of rupees on useless technology. An 
evaluation of its performance shows that two-thirds of its technologies could 
not be passed on to industry. The Science and Technology Policy ought to 
be reviewed in this regard. 
Madam, there is a joke going around in the Massachutes Institute 
of Technology that the In stitute is run by a Mafia from Kanpur, IIT meaning 
there are so many products from II T, Kanpur that they are playing a 
determining role there. Now, there is a problem being faced by our IITs 
that there are posts of 150 teachers lying vacant. If IITs cannot attract 
enough teachers, it only shows that th ere are shortfalls in our Policy. Our 
hon. Minister is a Pandit and he may be knowing the exact problem. 
The Science and Technology Policy, 2003, has rightly given a boost 
to our scientific and technological advancements, In fact, one of the 
heartening developments of the policy is  that while it aims at developing 
India through science and technology, it also aims to do so in a sustainable 
manner. Thus by integrating science and technology with environmental 
issues, it follows a balanced approach . Another significant feature of the 
policy is that it aims to ensure gender equality by promoting women in all 
science and technology activities and ensure their full and equal 
participation. In fact, one of the defin ing features of the late twentieth 
century, has been the awakening of wome n in the realisation of their rights, 
in practice and in full measure. They are launching their own movements to 
achieve their objectives. When the world was celebrating fifty years of the 
discovery of the DNA Double Helix, we  came to know how the role of a 
leading woman scientist - who also imm ensely contributed to the discovery 
- in .that path-breaking scientific endeavour, was never acknowledged. 
One of the critical issues being fa ced by scientific institutions is 
their redemption from the bureaucratic culture. They require full autonomy 
and a de-bureaucratised culture.   I welcome the provision in the policy that 
601 

RAJYA SABHA [13 August, 2003] 
all highly science-based Ministries/De partments of the Government will be 
run by scientists and technologists. 
It is also heartening to find that the policy calls for a certain 
percentage of the overall allocation of  each of the socio-economic Ministries 
to be devoted for relevant programmes and activities in science and 
technology. 
While all these are lofty goals en unciated in the policy, there are 
problems galore, which need to be addressed boldly. While we claim that 
we have emerged as one of the great economies in the world through our 
scientific and technological achievements,  we are painfully aware that there 
is a decline of interest among st udents for science education. Human 
resource development in the field of science and technology will be gravely 
affected if we cannot enthuse students to build up a career in science and 
technology. Our focus on ba sic research is getting diluted. Our scientific 
papers are not up to the mark. 
As such, we are not earmarking enough funds for science and 
technology. The policy airms at increasing it to two per cent of GDP by the 
end of the Tenth Plan. We have, I thin k, already completed two years of 
the Tenth Plan. Can we increase it to  one per cent by the middle of the 
Tenth Plan? The Government must come forward with a firm commitment 
to increase investments in this core sector of our country. 
Madam, the CAG Report for the year ending March, 2002, revealed 
that out of the 984 technologies develo ped by 23 laboratories of the CSIR, 
607 technologies, including 247 developed prior to 1996-97, had not been 
transferred. The laboratories were unab le to furnish specific information on 
the actual expenditure on the development of the technologies. Seventy- 
seven technologies were not found fit for commercialisation. Of these, 65 
cases were more than three-year-old. In the remaining 82 cases, 
negotiations for transfer were underway. The CSIR sustained a loss of 
Rs.99.31 lakhs due to its violations of the prescribed guidelines on 
technology transfer. 
There are many such critical paragraphs in the CAG Report relating 
to the Department of Biotechnology and the Department of Science and 
Technology. As far as the Department of Biotechnology is concerned, in 32 
projects, involving the release of Rs. 6.10 crores, the envisaged objectives 
602 

[13 August, 2003]                   RAJYA SABHA 
were not achieved, or, were only partially achieved. We do not have 
enough money for carrying forward our science and technology to the 
desired goal. But the sad fact is that  we are not properly utilising the 
available resources.   This is, indeed, unfortunate. 
The Government must properly monitor the spending of money by 
different scientific establishments.  The Parliamentary Standing Committee 
on Science and Technology has recommended that at the Revised 
Estimates stage the earmarked fund s of the respective scientific 
Departments should not be cut. While this  is important to do, we must also 
ensure that the money spent gives us good results. I hope that the 
Government' will carefully examine the CAG Report and take appropriate 
action. There is a welcome attempt in the Science Policy to create public 
awareness about science. Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru had written in the Discovery 
of India that in future there would be an increasing alliance between 
philosophy and science, out of which, scientific humanism will emerge. Our 
Science Policy must address to this  scientific humanism. Without this, 
science will only result in material development which will be devoid of 
human content. The world is turning to digital, herbal and spiritual ethos. 
India is rich in all these. Let us, therefore, harness these for our future 
progress. 
Madam, the views of the Govern ment on use of genetically 
modified seeds are not clear. Our farme rs have lost crores of rupees on 
opting for BT Cotton seeds. I request the Government to review its Science 
Policy in this regard, and concrete opinion should be given to help the 
farmers. 
Madam, India has the third largest scientific and technical 
manpower in the world. However, its research output does not match that 
claim. As far as research is concerned, India has slipped to the 21st place 
this year. The uneven speed of quality technical education accounts largely 
for the present state of research. The Science Policy should be reviewed 
accordingly. With these words, Madam, I whole-heartedly support the 
Science Policy of 2003. Thank you, Madam.

Government will have to consider specific measures to ensure and

[13 August, 2003]                  RAJYA SABHA 
STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Crash of Helicopter, engaged by ONGC in Mumbai High, 
on 11th August, 2003. 
The MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI RAM 
NAIK): Madam, I am indeed sorry to inform the hon. Members that in an 
extremely unfortunate accident, an MI-1 72 helicopter, chartered by the 
ONGC from the MESCO Airlines, crashed in the morning of11th August. 
The helicopter had taken off from the ONGC Helibase at Juhu, Mumbai at 
1137 hrs. The helicopter landed on the ONGC's Rig-Sagar Kiran, and took 
off from there at 12.15 hrs. to mo ve to another ONGC rig-Sagar Jyoti. 
Immediately on take-off from the Sagar Kiran, the helicopter crashed into 
the sea with 25 passengers, including 14 Officers and 8 Workmen of ONGC, 
3 contract employees and 4 crewmembers. 
Rescue operations were immediately initiated by launching rescue 
boat from the Sagar Kiran as well as by mobilising ONGC vessels, in the 
vicinity. Other helicopters, on charter, were also pressed into service for 
search and rescue. The Coast Guard and the Navy also joined the search 
and rescue operations within one hour. While 2 persons had been rescued, 
bodies of 3 persons, who died in the incident. had been recovered. The 
multipurpose supply vessels, deployed by the ONGC, have located the 
debris of the ill-fated helicopter on t he early morning of 12th August, at a 
depth of around 80 metres. In the early  hours, today, the helicopter was 
retrieved from the sea bottom and 22 bodies were found therein and 
identified. Search continues for remaining two bodies. 
As per the information available fr om the ONGC, the helicopter was 
reported to be airworthy, and no snag wa s reported at the time of take off 
on 11th August. 2003. The Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas had 
requested the Ministry of Civil Aviation,  the same day, to institute an enquiry 
to tobk into the circumstances of the incident. The Director General of Civil 
Aviation (DGCA) has accordingly order ed a statutory investigation by Shri 
V.K. Chandna, Deputy Director General.

RAJYA SABHA [13 August, 2003] 
In addition to the above, it has been decided to hold an 
independent inquiry by a three-member Committee which, inter alia, would 
look into the safety and security of life in offshore operations, especially air 
logistics, the maintenance, repairs and renovation of offshore structures and 
pipelines, hiring of helicopters and matters ancillary thereto. The Committee 
would report within three months. 
The CMD, ONGC, has been asked to draw up an emergency plan 
to further strengthen the safety measures for air transportation in the 
offshore, so as to make them fu lly comparable with the best global 
standards, in consultation with DGCA, within a fortnight. 
As per the ONGC's policy, the families of the deceased employees 
are entitled to financial compensation, ranging from Rs.14.3 lakh to 23.5. 
lakh, besides standard benefits, like Co ntributory Provident Fund, Gratuity, 
Leave Encashment and Pension under  Self-Financing Scheme etc. The 
contract employees are entitled to  compensation under the Workmen 
Compensation Act. I have announced an additional ex gratia benefit of Rs. 
5 lakh per employee. 
After hearing the sad news of the incident, I rushed to Mumbai by 
the first available flight and went  to Juhu Helibase of the ONGC. In 
Mumbai, I met representativ es of Officers and Empl oyees Associations and 
discussed the follow up measures with the CMD, ONGC and the Directors 
of the ONGC. 
On 11th August, 2003, the Collectives from Mumbai Region had 
written to me regarding a number of their demands, pending settlement of 
which the Offshore operations may be  affected from 0600 hours of 13 th 
August 2003. This charter was received la te at night on that day. I have 
urged the Collectives not to take any action which may adversely affect the 
oil and gas production from the Mumbai Offshore and thereby the national 
economy, at this critical juncture. I do hope that they would listen to my 
appeal and maintain normal production. Meanwhile, the ONGC 
management had approached the Mumbai High Court, which has directed 
the employees not to disrupt the production.

(a) whether it is a fact that in spite of a large number of changes in

Statement 
(a) to (c) Sir, in MTNL, Delhi, tne last issue of directory was published 
in 2000. In MTNL Mumbai, the last main directory was published in 
1999. The supplement 2001 has also been printed and distributed to 
subscribers in 2002 by MTNL Mumbai. 
In MTNL Delhi and Mumbai, tenders for six year period, are now 
being processed for bringing out directories every two years (main 
directory every alternate year and in the intervening period a 
supplementary directory). 
Meanwhile steps have been taken to make information available, 
which is normally contained in the printed directory, in other formats:- 
(i) IN CD ROM (priced concessionally at Rs. 50/-), which is updated 
at least once in a year and is av ailable at all Customer Service 
Centre/Sanchar Haat of MTNL. 
(ii) On internet website of MTNL, (www. mtnl.net.in) which is updated 
online. 
(iii) Toll-free Directory Information Service through '197'. 
According to information available, there is no directive of the Hon. 
Supreme Court of India to make directories available to the telephone 
subscribers annually. However, the guidelines of Department of Telecom, 
which are applicable to MTNL do provide that telephone directories be 
printed every alternative year an d in the intervening period, a 
supplementary directory be printed and made available to subscribers.

Production of sugar 
*344. SHRIMATI JAMANA DEVI BARUPAL: 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether sugar season showed an  excess of sugar production in 
2002-03 (October—September); 
(b) if so, what was the total sugar production in 2002-03; 
(c) whether in the sugar season of 2003-04, the assessment up-till 
nine months show that the 200 lakh tonnes mark has been crossed; 
(d) if so, whether the excess pro duction of sugar would create a 
problem in the country; 
(e) whether Government are considering to export more and more 
sugar during this year; 
(f) if so, the efforts being made; and 
(g) whether more export orders have been obtained? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHARAD YADAV): (a) to (g) Sugar production 
during the current 2002- 2003 (October—September) sugar season is 
estimated at about 200 lakh tonnes, as against 185.25 lakh tonnes 
during the 2001-2002 sugar season. As on 7th July, 2003, the total 
production during the 2002-2003 season was 198'.65 lakh tonnes 
(provisional). The sugar season 2003-2004 (October—September) has 
yet to commence. 
2. Sugar is exported under Open General Licence (OGL) and private 
parties/sugar mills export the same as per commercial judgement. 
The measures taken to promote the exports of sugar include: 
(i)  Quantitative restriction on export of sugar has been removed. 
(ii) Sugar meant for exports is exempted from the levy obligation. 
(iii) The quantity of sugar released for export is treated as advance 
freesale release to be adjusted in the freesale stocks of the 
sugar factories after a period of 18 months. 
23 

RAJA SABHA [ 14 August, 2003 ] 
(iv) Duty Entitlement Pass Book (DEPB) at the rate of 4% of the 
FOB value of export of sugar has been allowed. 
(v) The Sugar Development Fund Act, 1982 has been amended in 
order, inter alia, to utilize the Sugar Development Fund for 
defraying expenditure on internal transport charges and 
neutralization of ocean freight disadvantage to the sugar factories 
on export shipments of sugar. 
3. During the financial year 2002-2003, the exports of sugar have 
amounted to approximately 14.70 lakh tonnes.

Disparity in minimum wage 
*347. DR. ABRAR AHMED: 
SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: 
Will the Minister of LABOUR be pleased to state : 
(a) whether there is any disparity in rates of minimum wage in 
various regions of the country; if so, the details thereof; 
(b) the reasons for variation from region to region; and 
25 

RAJYA SABHA [14 August, 2003] 
(c) the steps being taken to bring in regional uniformity in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (SHRI SAHIB SINGH VERMA): (a) 
and (b) Yes, Sir. There is disparity in rates of minimum wages in various 
regions of the country, which is due to differences in socio-economic 
and agro-climatic conditions, prices of essential commodities, paying 
capacity, productivity and local conditions influencing the wage rate. 
The regional disparity in minimum wages is also attributed to the fact 
that both the Central and State Governments are the appropriate 
Government to fix, revise and enforce minimum wages in scheduled 
employments in their respective jurisdictions under the Minimum Wages 
Act, 1948. 
(c) In order to minimize the disparity in minimum wages in various 
regions of the country, the Central Government has issued guidelines 
for setting up Regional Minimum Wages Advisory Committees. In order 
to bring in uniformity in minimum wages, the Central Government mooted 
the concept of a national floor level minimum wage and fixed it at 
Rs. 35/- per day inl996 based on the recommendations of the National 
Commission on Rural Labour (1991) and subsequent rise in the price 
level. The national floor level wage is periodically revised based on the 
basis of increase in the Consumer Price Index. It was last revised to 
Rs. 50/- per day w.e.f. 1.9.2002. The States/UTs have been requested 
from time to time to ensure that the minimum wage in none of their 
scheduled employments is below the national floor level wage.

Disinvestment of BVFCL 
*355. SHRI DRUPAD BORGOHAIN: Will the Minister of 
DISINVESTMENT be pleased to state : 
(a) whether it is a fact that Brahmapu tra Valley Fertilizer Corporation 
Ltd. (BVFCL) is going to be disinvested; 
(b) if so, the details of the proposal; and 
(c) what has necessitated the disinvestment when Government had 
revamped the unit expending more than four hundred crores of rupees 
and bifurcated it from the sick HFCL? 
THE MINISTER OF DISINVESTM ENT (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE) : 
(a) to (c) The Disinvestment Commission in its 20th Report (May, 2003) 
has inter alia recommended that given the history of losses and poor 
envisaged profitability of Brahmaputra Valley Fertilizer Corporation limited 
(BVFCL), the Government should disinvest up to 74% of its equity in 
BVFCL to a strategic partner through the competitive bidding route. 
In accordance with its declared policy, the Government's equity in all 
non-strategic Central Public Sector Undertakings (CPSUs), irrespective 
of being profit making or loss incurring, is to be brought down to 26% or 
below in generality of cases. BVFCL operates in the non-strategic sector. 
The Government has not taken a decision on the recommendations of 
the Disinvestment Commission.

SHRIMATIN.RDURGA:

scheme, the beneficiary's contribution is 10% of the project cost. In 
case of SC/ST/other weaker sections, beneficiary's contribution is 5% of 
the project cost. This scheme is being implemented through Public Sector 
banks, Regional Rural Banks etc.

Exemption of officers from liability 
2561. SHRI MURLI DEORA: Will the Minister of COMMUNICATIONS 
AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state : 
(a) whether sections 6 and 43 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1893 
stipulates exemption to officers from liability of loss, delay, misdelivery 
and damage; 
(b) whether this exemption is absolu te and if not, why the officers 
are not charged with dereliction of duty and deficiency; and 
(c) whether Government propose to amend such obnoxious sections 
which creates hurdles in the efficien t administration of the Department 
and if not, the reasons therefor ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (SHRI S U. 
THIRUNAVUKKARASAR): (a) and (b) The Indian Post Office Act is actually 
of 1898. Section 6 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898, provides that no 
officer of the Post Office shall incur any liability by reason of any such 
loss, misdelivery, delay or damage, unless he has caused the same 
fraudulently or by his wilful act or default. This expemption is not absolute. 
76 

[ 14 August, 2003 ] RAJYA SABHA 
Suitable notice including disciplinary action is taken against officials 
wherever necessary for dereliction of duty and deficiency. Section 43 
does not stipulate any exemption. 
(c) Does not arise in view of (a) and (b) above.

Recommendations made by "High level Committee on long-term 
grain policy" 
2605. SHRI NANDI YELLAIAH :Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state : 
(a) the status report of implementation by Government as on date, 
with regard to various recommendations and proposals as made through 
a report by the "High level Committee on long-term grain policy", July 
2002; and 
(b) what remedial measures are being taken by Government towards 
greater production and proper security of Food Distribution in view of the 
report having shown at all India level, much decrease in food production, 
area of cultivation and yield per hectare from 1999 which is a warning 
signal for a rapid negative growth of production? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION ( SHRI SUBHASH 
MAHARIA : (a) Government has examined the major recommendations 
121 

RAJYA SABHA [ 14 August, 2003 ] 
made by the High Level Committee on Long Term Grain Policy (HLC) 
constituted under the Chairmanship of Prof. Abhijit Sen. 
The action taken with regard to the main recommendations of the 
HLC are as under:— 
(i) The HLC has made several recommendations with regard to the 
Fixing of the Minimum Support Prices of foodgrains. The 
Government has, however, decided that the present Minimum 
Support Price Regime should continue. 
(ii) With regard to the recommendation of the HLC for introduction 
of a universal Public-Distribution System (PDS) with uniform 
Central Issue Prices (CIPs). It is felt by the Government that 
the targeted PDS was introduced in June, 1997 with a view to 
target the unprivileged sections  of society, as the earlier 
universal PDS did not adequately focus on the poor and hungry 
and had an urban bias. Under the TPDS, the families Below the 
Poverty Line (BFL) have been identified and foodgrains are 
supplied to the BPL families at highly subsidized rates at less 
than 50% of the economic cost at the scale of 35 Kg. per family 
per month. The introduction of a universal PDS will result in the 
PDS losing its focus on meeting the needs of the poor. 
(iii) The HLC has recommended that for an effective foodgrains 
management system, it is necessary to liquidate the excess 
accumulation of stocks. To achieve this, several measures have 
been taken as a result of which stocks have reduced from 630 
lakh tonnes as on 1st July, 2002 to 352 lakh tonnes as on 
1st July, 2003. 
(iv) The HLC also recommended disposal of old stocks and stock 
procured under relaxed quality st ocks. As a result of measures 
taken for disposal of such stocks, over 80% of current stocks 
are less than 2 years old. 
(v) As recommended by the HLC, the coverage of households has 
been increased by an additional 50 lakh persons with focus on 
the destitute population under Antyodaya Anna Yojana. 
122 

[ 14 August, 2003 ] RAJYA  SABH A 
(vi) The allocation under the Sampoorna Gramin RojgarYojana(SGRY) 
and Special Component'of the SGRY scheme has been 
considerably enhanced as recommended by the HLC. 
(vii) To improve functioning of the PDS instructions have already been 
issued for strict implementation of PDS Control Order to ensure 
greater transparency in the working of the PDS and reduction in 
the diversion of foodgrains under the PDS. Guidelines have been 
issued for the involvement of the Panchayat: Raj Institutions in 
the implementation of the TPDS. 
(b) The agricultural production in the country shows a long term upward 
trend, albeit with fluctuations due to weather aberrations. A major factor 
for sustaining this growth, especially in foodgrains production, has been 
the procurement policy under Minimum Support Price operations. 
Government is also implementing the following schemes to further improve 
the production of cereals :— 
(i)   Integrated Cereals Development Programme in Rice Based 
Cropping Systems Areas (ICDP-Rice) 
(ii)   Integrated Cereals Deve lopment Programme in Wheat Based 
Cropping System Areas (ICDP-Wheat) 
(iii) Integrated Cereals Developm ent Programme in Coarse Cereals 
Based Cropping System Areas (ICDP-Coarse Cereals) 
From October, 2002 these schemes have heen subsumed under the

commercial partnerships. They regularly undertake promotional

 † 2654. SHRI LAJPAT RAI: 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL:

(SHRI VINOD KHANNA): (a) to (d) The India-China Joint Working 
Group (JWG) on the Boundary Question was constituted in 1988. It 
has met 14 times. The 14th meeting of the JWG was held in New Delhi 
on 21st November, 2002. 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi 
165 

RAJYA SABHA [14 August, 2003] 
India and China seek a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable 
settlement of the boundary question through peaceful consultations. 
They signed an agreement on the Maintenance of Peace and Tranquility 
along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in the India-China Border Areas 
in 1993 and a second agreement on Confidence Building Measures in 
the Military Field along the Line of Actual Control in the India-China 
Border Areas in 1996. These two Agreements provide an institutional 
framework for the maintenance of peace and tranquility in the border 
areas. The process of clarification of the LAC has started within existing 
mechanisms. Maps of the LAC in the Middle Sector have been 
exchanged. Discussions have commenced on clarification of the LAC in 
the Western Sector of the India-China boundary 
During the 14th meeting of the JWG, both sides reviewed the 
ongoing process of LAC clarification. They also continued discussions 
on further confidence Building M easures. Both sides agreed, inter alia, 
on the need to substantially enhance trade and economic relations, 
cultural and people-to-people exchanges. Both sides also reviewed 
the functioning of the existing dialogue mechanisms, such as on counter 
terrorism and security, and agreed to establish a dialogue mechanism 
between the two Foreign Offices on policy planning . Regional and 
international issues were also discussed.

Gloomy picture of Indian economy 
2677. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH : Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state : 
(a) whether World Bank Development Policy Review's assessment 
has recently painted a gloom and doom picture of Indian economy; 
(b) if so, the detail of their findings; and 
(c) Government's reaction thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) and (b) The World Bank in 
its development policy review entitled 'India: Sustaining Reform, 
Reducing Poverty' released on July 14, 2003, while acknowledging that 
India's growth over the past two decades has been one of the world's 
highest among large countries, has expressed concern over the 
deterioration in the fiscal position of the Centre and States. The Review 
observed that rising deficits and worsening public expenditure 
composition has limited the prosp ect for accelerating growth and 
poverty reduction. 
(c) The Government is conscious of the need for reduction in fiscal 
deficit and promoting investment for productive purposes. Fiscal 
consolidation is one of the five prio rities addressed in the Union Budget 
for 2003-04. The Budget has proposed a number of initiatives, such as, 
promoting infrastructure development by leveraging public money through 
private sector participation, promoting private investment and measures 
aimed at fiscal consolid ation. These initiatives, inter alia, are expected 
to have a positive influence on the growth of the economy.

2692. PROF M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of SMALL 
SCALE INDUSTRIES be pleased to state : 
(a) the steps taken to develop and boost the SSIs during the last four 
years; 
(b) the number of persons employed in SSI during the said period; 
and 
(c) the number of SSIs set up in the country during the last four 
years, State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE FOR SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (SHRI 
TAPAN SIKDAR): (a) The Comprehensive Policy Package for the Small 
Scale Industries and Tiny Sector was announced on 30th August, 2000 
which aims to ensure enhanced fiscal and credit support, better 
infrastructural and marketing facilities and incentives for technology 
upgradation. Some of the significant measures included in the policy 
package and those taken during last 4 years to develop and boost the 
SSIs are:— 
(i) Raising the excise exemption limit for SSis on first clearances 
of Rs. 50 lakhs to Rs. 100 lakhs, on annual turnover upto 
Rs. 300 lakhs. 
(ii) Launching of Cr edit Guarantee Fund Scheme for providing 
collateral free loans upto Rs. 25 lakhs. 
(iii)   Raising the composite loan  limit from Rs. 10 lakhs to 
Rs.25 lakhs.

(iv) Launching of Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme for 
technology upgradation providing 12% capital subsidy for 
technology upgradation in selected sub-sectors. 
(v) Enhancing the Project cost limit upto Rs. 50 lakhs under 
National Equity Fund Scheme. 
(vi) A new Market Development Assistance (MDA) Scheme 
launched providing financial assistance from participating in 
international fairs, exhibitions and reimbursement of expenses 
incurred on adopting Bar-coding by EAN India. 
(vii) Extending ISO 9000 Certification Reimbursement Scheme to 
Tenth Five Year Plan and also providing assistance for acquiring 
ISO 14000 Certification. 
(viii) Providing financial assistance to SSI Associations for setting 
up of testing facilities; 
(ix) The modified Integrated Infrastructural Development (IID) 
Scheme to provide for 50% reservation for rural areas and 
50% for tiny units. 
(x) Issuance of revised guidelines by Reserve Bank of India for 
rehabilitation of sick SSI units and revival of potentially viable 
units, based on Kohli Committee recommendations. 
(xi) In addition, earlier incentives and Schemes for enhancing flow 
of credit, technology upgradation, marketing promotion, etc.

Need to remove discrimination in age limit for Air Hostesses of Air India for 
on-board duty 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Now, we will take up Special Mentions. 
Shri Dinesh Trivedi. 
SHRI DINESH TRIVEDI (West Bengal): Madam. Deputy Chairperson, 
I will be extremely brief and very pointed. I am raising the question of 
discriminating the women air-hostesse s on the basis of gender. Madam, 
recently a directive was published by the Government of India about which I 
came to know through a newspaper. It was later confirmed by the Air- 
Hostesses' Association also. Recently, the Ministry of Civil Aviation has 
given a directive to Air India that their air-hostesses ...(Interruptions)... 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Do you remember your Special Mention 
by heart? 
SHRI DINESH TRIVEDI: Madam. I had my papers, but I did not 
know that it would be taken up today. However, I do remember it because 
I have done some study on it and I have done some work. 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Okay. 
SHRI DINESH TRIVEDI: So, Madam, Air India was given a directive 
that air-hostesses who reach the age of 58 should be grounded, and, may 
be given the ground duties. Please unders tand this that it is only for the 
air-hostesses and not for the cabin atte ndants; their male counter-parts. 
So. Madam, the difference here is that the female air-hostesses, who are 
females obviously, should get some ground job after the age of 50 years, 
and their male counter-parts could cont inue after the age of 58. Madam, in 
this very House, you have been a champion in promoting the cause of 
women. There is the Women's Empowerment Committee as well. We have 
article 40, which protects the righ ts of individuals and there is no 
discrimination based on sex.  creed, caste, colour, religion, race and place of 
birth.   But here, Madam, instead of giving more encouragement to women, 
214 

[14 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
we are just giving them ground job, a fter they reach the age of 50, which is 
very unfortunate. I fully appreciate that the job requirement in an aircraft is 
that of high skill and good health. There is no problem, as far as these air- 
hostesses are concerned. They could go through medical check-ups once 
in six- months or a year, whatever is the recommendation. Being a pilot, I 
know a little bit about flying. We have a lot of capable women pilots who 
are not only co-piloting the aircraft, but they are flying as commander as 
well. We have several flights also where both the commander and the co- 
pilot are women and they fly the aircraft very successfully, with full 
confidence and safety. If women pilots are allowed to fly a plane, why can't 
they serve the passengers after the age of 50? What all I am trying to say, 
in conclusion, Madam, is that Air Indi a should give the directives, or the 
Ministry should give the directives that whoever wants to retire at the age of 
50, for whatever reason, other than medical, they could be permitted to 
retire and get a ground job till the age of 58, that is, till the retirement. 
Lastly, the Indian Airlines, which is al so a State-owned Airline, does not 
discriminate. For them, the retirement ag e, as of now, is 58, if there is a 
recent change, I do not know. So, Madam, I will appeal through you - you 
are a champion of the cause of women- to give some directives and I hope 
the Government would change this step.

Recycling and better management of plastic waste 
SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA (Jharkhand): Madam, 
the plastic industry in India contribu tes more than two million tonnes of 
plastic to our waste stream. These include bottles, food packagings, 
cement bags, medical disposals, all of  which become waste with just one 
use. This industry is growing at 12-15 per cent annually. It is good that the 
industry is growing, because of wh ich the employment opportunities are 
increasing, so also the GDP. But at what cost? The whole country, the 
entire landscape, is being littered with plastic bottles and thin plastic bags. 
They keep flying everywhere causing eye-sores to many people. Actually it 
is not the use of plastic that is caus ing the problem, but the indiscriminate 
waste that is being created which ha s become a matter of serious concern 
for the environment. It is true that the plastic has changed our lives, and it 
is affordable even to a poor man. But the waste is choking the animals, 
including the cow, and the soil. T here is no waste management of the 
plastic waste in our country. People are not habituated to properly throw 
away the used plastic things including bottles and bags. The Government 
has banned the manufacture of thin plastic bags. But this alone is not 
sufficient. 
In many Western countries including Sweden, Norway and Germany, 
the plastic manufacturers are forced to collect plastic waste and recycle it. 
The European Union says, "The producers are responsible". Management 
of waste plastic and recycling of it ar e essential now in our country. Unless 
these things are done, the problem cannot be solved. It is difficult to stop 
manufacture of plastic altogether, but waste management and recycling are 
very well in our hands. The Government should, therefore, take necessary 
steps for recycling of the plastic waste and better management of the 
plastic waste.

Need to use Solar Cooking Systems for Mid-Day Meals Scheme in 
Andhra Pradesh 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO (Andhra Pradesh): Madam, the 
Government of Andhra Pradesh, with the objective of universalisation of 
elementary education, is implementing the Mid-Day Meal Scheme, and 
giving hot, cooked food to the children of I-VII standards in the Government 
schools, local bodies' schools and the Government-aided primary and 
upper-primary schools in Andhra Pradesh; the Scheme has a coverage of 
74.59 lakh children in the year 20 02-03. The implementation agencies for 
this scheme are the DWCRA, the Co mmunity Development Agencies, the 
NGOs, etc. The State Government has  also provided funds to all the 
District Collectors for the construction of additional rooms in schools to be 
used as kitchens. The Government is al so ensuring provision of 300 calories 
and 8-12 grams of protein content per child everyday, with boiled eggs and 
bananas once in a week. Apart from this, the Government is thinking of 
introducing two more recipes -- hot pongal and tomato bhat - very shortly. 
The cost of it comes to Re.1 and Rs.1.10 respectively per child, which is far 
more than 0.5 paise spent by many other States. All these things have 
been substantiated by a survey conduc ted by the Centre for Development 
Economics. The Scheme is being implemented in 69,615 schools. The total 
number of kitchens running  on  gas is 48,056 and the total  number of

kitchens running on the other fuel' is 21,559. So, in order to make the 
Scheme more effective and successful, there is need to introduce Solar 
Concentrating Cooking Systems in all the kitchens that are using the other 
fuel'. The Ministry of Non-Convent ional Energy Sources has sanctioned 
such systems to some of the schools in Rajasthan. Hence, I beseech the 
Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources to immediately sanction Solar 
Concentrating Cooking Systems in all the 21,559 kitchens which do not have 
gas connections. 
Need to review the guidelines of Prime Minister's Rojgar Yojana 
SHRI C. PERUMAL (Tamil Nadu): Madam Deputy Chairperson, the 
Prime Minister's Rojgar Yojana was launched to help the unemployed youth 
to set up self-employment ventures. This scheme is specially meant for the 
educated unemployed who constitute 40 per cent of the unemployed 
people. There are clear guidelines in re spect of sanction of loans under the 
Prime Minister's Rojgar Yojana. But, the nationalised banks do not observe 
these guidelines. The banks have unwritten rules and find ways to refuse 
loan to the unemployed youth who approach them. One of the salient 
features of this scheme is the wa iving the collateral security. The 
matriculation certificate of the person  applying for loan is the guarantee 
required under the guidelines. For se lf-employment projects up to rupees 
one lakh, no collateral security is required. But, the banks do not follow 
these guidelines. As a result, the poor unemployed youth are not able to get 
the benefit of the scheme.  I request the Government to issue firm directive 
to all the nationalised banks to sanction loans without asking for security. 
The requirement of collateral security for loans above rupees one lakh 
should also be waived. Otherwise, the very purpose of this scheme will be 
defeated. Since the trend of higher gr owth of unemployment of educated 
youth continues, it is necessary to see that the Prime Minister's Rojgar 
Yojana is implemented in letter and spirit. Therefore, the Government should 
review the guidelines and direct the banks to sanction loans on the basis of 
matriculation certificate of  the applicant, without the requirement of any form 
of security. Such a step alone will achieve the target, as spelt out in the 
scheme. Thank you, Madam.

prices of steel 
SHRI LAJPAT RAI (Punjab): Madam Deputy Chairperson, my 
Special Mention is about the disturbing situation having developed because

had been rising during the last one year. When would steel authorities in 
India rise to the occasion and respond to the critical situation as obtained in 
the steel-consuming industry, especially in the small-scale sector? A large 
number of small-scale units engaged in the production of cycle and its 
parts, auto parts, hand tools, hardware and fans, etc., have already 
succumbed to the pressure of the steep rise in the price of steel; and many 
more are on the verge of closure. 
Undoubtedly, the Government have been encouraging the small-scale 
sector and the industry has also been responding through appreciable 
development and employment generation, but looking at the situation being 
faced by the steel-based industry on acc ount of steep hike in the price of 
steel effected by the steel-producing giants, both in the public and the 
private sector, had virtuall y placed the small-scale sector in India in a Catch 
22 situation. 
The irony of fate is that the steel-based industry in the small-scale 
sector in India has been incapacitated to  face the competition with China in 
particular, for the reason that steel ex ported by Indian steel giants to China 
is cheaper than that sold  by them in the country  where the prices are 
exorbitant. The steel giants/exporte rs, by adding export benefits to the 
export price get more than fully comp ensated. The export price happened 
to be around Rs.14,000 per metric tonne and the price charged in the

woes of the small-scale sector. It is beyond comprehension why the 
authorities concerned have not concentrat ed on the solution to the problem, 
and may it be expected that immediat e meetings with industrialists 
concerned would be convened to find a solution.

Nutritional standard 
*373. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state : 
(a) whether it is a fact that National  Institute of Nutrition has conducted 
a survey to assess the nutritional standards of various States; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the National Nutrition Monitoring Bureau 
(NNMB) has undertaken a survey to st udy the nutritional levels in the 
drought affected States; 
(c) if so, the findings thereof with special reference to Andhra Pradesh; 
(d) the impact of Food for Work and Targeted Public Distribution System 
(TPDS) on the nutritional levels among the poor in Andhra Pradesh; and 
(e) the steps taken to correct the nutritional imbalance among the 
poor sections? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI R. RAJA): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the 
Table of the House. 
28 

[18 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Statement 
(a) to (e) The Indian council of Medical Research's National Nutrition 
Monitoring Bureau (with the Central Reference Laboratory at the National 
Institute of Nutrition at Hyderabad) has undertaken a survey during May- 
July, 2003 to assess the diet and nu tritional status of population in 
the drought affected areas of the nine States, namely, Andhra Pradesh, 
Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, Gujarat, 
Rajasthan and Chhattisgarh. Based on preliminary findings, it has been 
reported that there have been no star vation deaths in these States. As 
regards the State of A ndhra Pradesh, about 82% of the households were 
availing one or the other development  programmes, such as Sampoorna 
Grameen Rozgar Yojana, Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS), 
Antodaya Anna Yojana, Annapurna and old age/widow pension programmes. 
Regarding the Food for Work and TPDS in the State of Andhra Pradesh, 
about 41 % of the households reportedly participated in Food-for-Work 
programme, while 64% availed of TPDS. These programmes, alongwith 
other developmental programmes such as old age/widow/Disabled 
Pensions, Annapurna, Antodaya Anna Yojana, Integrated Child 
Development Services (ICDS), Mid-day Meal programmes etc., may have 
averted more deleterious effects of dr ought on health and nutritional status 
of the community. 
Several nutrition intervention programmes like, Integrated Child 
Development Services (ICDS), progra mme for distribution of vitamin A 
and Iron folic acid are being implemented. In addition, the programmes 
such as widow/old age pension, An todaya Anna Yojana (AAY), Targeted 
Public Distribution System (TPDS)  and Food-for-Work Programme which 
are being implemented are targeted towards the poor to improve their 
nutritional status.

Disease prone areas 
*362. SHRI DATTA MEGHE: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state : 
(a) whether Government have identified the areas prone to deadly 
diseases like malaria.encephalitis and dengue; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the action plan/measures taken so far to contain the diseases? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI 
SUSHMA SWARAJ) : (a) to (c) Yes,  Sir. Based on epidemiological 
consideration, the areas prone to Ma laria have been identified. North- 
Eastern States, predominantly tribal areas in 8 States, namely, Andhra 
Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat,  Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, 
Maharashtra, Orissa and Rajasthan, as  well as some pockets of West 
Bengal, Goa, Uttar Pradesh and Karnatak a, have been identified as areas 
prone to Malaria. 
Japanese Encephalitis has been re ported from 24 States and UTs 
but 14 States are prone for outbreaks. Such outbreaks have been noticed 
frequently in certain districts of Uttar Pradesh and Andhra Pradesh. 
The risk of Dengue is present throughout the country. Urban areas 
are at higher risk due to increased use of water storage tanks, water 
coolers, tyre dumps and constructi on activities which create breeding 
sites for mosquitoes. Outbreaks of dengue are reported in Kerala, 
Karnataka, Maharashtra and Delhi in recent years. 
Prevention and control of these vector borne diseases including 
outbreaks is the responsib ility of the State Govern ments. The Government 
of India assists the State Governme nts by way of providing technical 
support and sending expert teams to the affected areas of the States. 
In so far as Malaria is concerned, National Anti Malaria Programme 
(NAMP) is in operation as a Category-ll Centrally Sponsored Scheme. 
However, taking into account that t he North-Eastern States are highly 
endemic to Malaria, 100% Central assistance is being provided to the 
States from December, 1994. 
A World Bank supported Enhanced Malaria Control Project (EMCP) 
covering 1045 PHCs in 100 districts with tribal population in the 8 above 
39 

RAJYA SABHA [18 August, 2003] 
mentioned States is bei ng implemented since Sept ember, 1997. Funds to 
meet the operational cost are also bei ng provided to the States apart from 
providing insecticides, drugs, larvicides etc. under the project. 
Strategies adopted for control of Malaria include:- 
• Early case detection and prompt treatment. 
• Selective vector control. 
• Promotion of personal protection methods. 
• Early detection and containment of epidemics. 
• Information, Education and Communication towards personal 
prevention and community participation. 
• Institutional and Management Capacity Building, Trained Manpower 
Development and efficient Management Information System (MIS). 
The strategies for controlling Dengue include:- 
• Disease and vector surveillance. 
• Reduction of vector with community participation. 
• Effective case management. 
• Information, Education and Communication measures. 
• Epidemic preparedness and early response. 
Strategies being adopted to control Japanese Encephalitis include:- 
1. Vector control by insecticidal spraying with appropriate insecticide 
in high risk areas. 
2. Early diagnosis and proper management to reduce fatality. 
3. Health Education. 
4. Training of Medical Personnel and professionals.

THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION [MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B. C. KHANDURI]: (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) In the recent past, a number of issues relating to Delhi such as

(c) and (d) The Master Plan of Delhi is formulated in accordance with
