Statement 
Guidelines for Master Plan for Delhi-2021 
In Delhi the approach of planned urban development has been practised 
since the decade of the sixties, which is incorporated in the first and the 
second Master Plans. It is time that the third Master Plan is concretized 
which should incorporate the lessons learnt from the experience of the 
last four decades as well as policy departures to secure proper development 
of Delhi in its emerging context. 
2. In the last four decades Delhi has developed into a massive 
metropolis which has provided shelter to millions of people who have 
arrived here as a part of the phenomenon of rural-urban change and in 
search of jobs and opportunities. The national capital region has also 
developed impressively, though with a spatial distortion in the sense that 
only the Delhi Metropolitan Area (DMA) towns adjoining Delhi have 
developed and not the National Capital Region (NCR) towns with a spatial 
44 

[18 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
gap from Delhi. Within Delhi large areas have developed in a planned 
manner but large areas have also grown outside the framework of the 
Master Plan. The need now is to take into account all that has happened 
and to try and introduce approaches wh ich will ensure that its further 
development is inconsonance with t he requisites of modern living and 
within acceptable environmental parameters. A very important concern 
will have to be orderly incorporati on of the poor people who migrate from 
the hinter land. 
3. The Ministry is aware that the Delhi Development Authority has 
been actively engaged in evolving the Third Master Plan and that it has 
held numerous exercises to involve various sections of opinion. The NCR 
Planning Board has also been engaged in a similar exercise for the national 
capital region. The Ministry wishes to provide the following guidelines to 
DDA in the hope that they will be of help in finalizing the draft of the plan 
at an early date. 
4. Urban expansion in the two prev ious plans has been based on the 
policy of large scale acquisition and di sposal of land by DDA. The positive 
gains and the negative fallout of this  policy are before us. On the negative 
side, it has, quite contrary to the in tention of the policy, resulted in the 
creation of a large number of unaut horised colonies and J.J. clusters. 
Since, under the policy, the farmers c ould only get the price of compulsory 
acquisition, they have tended to resist acquisition and, in many cases, to 
sell their lands for unauthorized colonization through the intermediation of 
colonizers and land mafia. When the farmers could not escape acquisition 
they felt deprived of their share in the value addition that occurs upon 
conversion of agricultural land to urban land. A major drawback in the 
approach arose from the substantia l time gap between acquisition, 
development and disposal of land, during which period it remains an 
invitation to encroachment. Aided by inadequate protection of the acquired 
land and weak enforcement of building regulations, a large number of 
unauthorized colonies and J.J. clusters have come up and characterize 
a substantial part of Delhi today. It is necessary to seek a suitable 
alternative to the past policy of la rge scale acquisition and disposal of 
land by DDA. The Ministry is happy t hat in a number of seminars held on 
the subject progress has been made towards evolving an alternative 
approach which would obviate the taking of land by DDA ahead of the 
commencement of development and which would also provide the farmers 
45 

RAJYA SABHA [18 August, 2003] 
a fair share in the development urban land. The aproach should also give 
the private sector its due role in urban development and housing. Before 
it is considered for incorporation in the new Master Plan the alternative 
approach has to be worked out in its details, particularly giving regard to 
the interests of the poor migrants.  Also, regulatory and enforcement 
arrangements will have to be strengthened to prevent any further growth 
of unauthorised colonies and J. J. cluster. 
5. The growth of DMA towns has resulted in deflecting some of the 
accretion that would have otherwise  occurred to Delhi's population. 
However, a stronger effort is needed to check the growth of migration to 
the national capital in the future. The National Capital Region Plan has to 
be much more dynamic. The recent su ccess in harmonization of tax rates 
among the NCR States needs to be carried forward into economic and 
industrial linkage policies. Transportation linkages (including sub-urban 
rail links and by-pass expressways) have to be built. The synergy between 
the NCR Plan and Delhi's Master Plan has to be strengthened. 
6. The areas of irregular development in Delhi must be expeditiously 
and effectively incorporated in th e mainstream of urban development. 
Regularization of unauthorized colonies should not just be nominal but 
also effective, which means that, after due planning, infrastructure of 
roads and streets, parks, drinking wa ter, drainage, sewage disposal, 
electricity, schools, medical and communi ty facilities etc. must be provided. 
The operation of regularization has to be so conducted that the residents 
may be able to secure sanction of building plans and to build/rebuild in 
accordance with the municipal laws. 
7. A major issue that has been debat ed is that of segregated land use 
versus flexible land use. While adhering to the requisites of environment, 
the current thinking is in favour of flexible land use, which reaps the 
synergies between workplace, residence and transportation as also 
between complementary vocations. Ideally, land use should be responsive 
to the dynamics of the market. It may be necessary to consider the 
approach of flexible land use so that solutions can be found to several of 
the questions that have been vexed in recent years:— 
(a) Mixed residential and commercia l land use in many more areas 
by suitably extending the provisions that have existed in this 
behalf in the previous Master Plan concerning shops etc. in 
residential areas. 
46 

[18 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) Commercial/office use of industrial premises keeping in view its 
environmental benefits and economic desirability. 
(c) Concentration of industries to the extent of 70% or more in some 
non-industrial areas making them virtually industrial in use. 
8. A major the me of the new Mast er Plan should be redevelopment of 
(a) old and degraded areas (while taking care that buildings of heritage 
value are protected and conserved) and (b) areas that have developed 
unauthorizedly.The existing legal and procedural barriers to redevelopment, 
whether contained in the slum related l egislation or in the municipal laws, 
need to be reviwed and positive incentives  (such as higher FAR in the old 
city and the "special area") can be considered. 
9. The existing slums/JJ clusters ought to be ameliorated by a 
judicious mix of relocation and in-situ development.

DDA, particularly those which have become aged, has r epeatedly arisen. 
Permission is being given for some specific additions/alterations which 
do not impinge on structural safety. In the new Master Plan the matter 
needs to be addressed in a wider pe rspective. For instance, the DDA 
colonies, through proper use of Apartments Act (which can be suitably 
modified to remove its deficiencies), which may be converted into self 
managing residential.communities, which may even be given rights for 
reconstructing the outdated and derelict structures by making use of the 
incentive of higher FAR now permitted, consequent to the 
recommendations of the Malhotra Committee. 
11. An opportunity for redevelopment in Delhi is offered on the two 
sides of the metro rail routes, about 70 kilometres of which will become 
available in the first phase to be completed in 2005. That will be the best 
use of the synergy between transportation and urban development. A 
practical approach of providing the requi site infrastructure on the sides of 
tne tracks, say to a depth of about ha lf a kolometre, and of permitting a 
suitably enhanced FAR in construction could be devised and included in 
the Master Plan. 
12.The issue of vertical constructi on (including that below the ground) 
needs to be seen in the light of techni cal devices which are now available. 
Moreover, vertical construction need not mean higher density; in fact, it 
may reduce the proportion of ground coverage and enhance greens and 
common spaces. 
47 

RAJYA SABHA [18 August, 2003] 
13. In providing housing, both the cooperative sector and DDA have 
made sizeable contributions. The approac h how needs to be reoriented by 
providing an active role also to the pr ivate sector and also by incorporating 
the involvement of numerous instit utions engaged in the business of 
finance for housing. 
Affordable housing has to be brought wi thin the reach of economically 
weaker sections and of new migrants to the capital. It must also be realized 
that, with the emergence of alternatives in DMA towns, housing is no

14. A major issue confronting the planned development of Delhi is the

norms. There is a growing variation between the plan for Delhi and the

15. Much investment has been made in recent years in transportation

Geneva meeting of developing countries 
*380. DR. AKHILESH DAS: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that about 20 developing countries including 
South Africa and Sri Lanka led by India met at Geneva, and stressed the 
need for addressing the concerns of developing countries, particularly 
their agriculture related concerns  about protectionist policies and 
programmes of the developed countries, under the WTO regime; 
(b) if so, the response of the countries thereto; and 
56 

[18 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) the prospects of implementation of the Doha declaration? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI ARUN 
JAITLEY): (a) to (c) As part of the on-going negotiations on World Trade 
Organisation (WTO) Agreement on Agricult ure India along with the United 
Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) had organised 
a meeting at Nyon near Geneva on  25 June, 2003 of like-minded 
developing countries to discuss issu es of common interest, namely, the 
instruments of Special Products (SP Products), and the new Special 
Safeguard Mechanism (SSM) proposed for developing countries to enable 
them to address food security and rural development and/or livelihood 
concerns. This meeting also consid ered domestic support modalities for 
developed countries in order to better address the distortions in world 
agriculture markets, and sanitary and phyto-sanitary measures being used 
by some major trading partners to deny market access in products of 
export interest to developing countries. 
In the negotiations, so far, divergence among Members of the WTO 
on key issues are evident, including on the levels of ambition as regards 
the further commitments in  the three pillars of the negotiations, namely, 
market access, domestic support and export competition. The Cairns 
Group (consisting of major agricultural products' exporting developed 
and developing countries, including Australia, Brazil, Canada, Malaysia 
and South Africa) and the US favour steep tariff reductions on imports, 
substantial reduction in domestic s upport, and elimination of direct export 
subsidies, the European Communities  (EC) and its candidate States, 
Japan, Switzerland, Norway, and Korea favour moderate tariff reductions 
based on the Uruguay Round approach, and have linked their flexibility 
on support and protection in the farm sector with incorporation on non- 
trade concerns, such as animal welfare, in the negotiations. Countries 
which have recently acceded to the WT O, such as China, Croatia, Jordan 
and Oman, favour exemption from further commitments, having already 
made substantial commitm ents across all WTO Agreements during their 
process of accession. Developing count ries which are net importers of 
food attach importance to improved availability of food at affordable prices, 
and therefore, do not insist upon elimination of export, subsidies. Small 
economies with a heavy reliance on preferential trading arrangements 
with Members, such as the EC and US, for economic development and 
growth, support continuation of preferential access to these markets. 
57 

RAJYA SABHA [18 August, 2003] 
Least developed countries have been seeking complete exemption from 
any further commitments in support or protection of agriculture. While a 
number of developing countries support  flexibility to safeguard food and 
livelihood security through the application of SP products and SSM 
instruments, most developed and some developing country Members 
insist that these instruments should not be used to deny market access. 
As may be seen, while there are common interests and concerns 
between India and some other WTO Members, divergences in positions 
remain on the level of ambition as well as on key issues in the negotiations. 
The negotiations are scheduled to be concluded by 1 January, 2005.

2702. DR. A.R. KIDWAI: Will th e Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether European Union has stuck to its stand that the farm export 
subsidies can not be reduced and to push forward proposals for the 
negotiations on the possible multilateral agreements on investment; 
(b) if so, whether recently at Nyon near Geneva, a meeting was held 
with the developing countries on agriculture and the issues of special 
products, special safeguard measures and subsidies discussed; 
(c) whether Government have decided to accord top priority to increase 
market access for products of dairy, cereals, sugar, meat, poultry, fruits 
and vegetables; and 
(d) if so, the steps Government propose to take to see that WTO 
recommendations are fully met? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI CHENNAMANENI VIDY ASAGAR RAO): (a) In the on- 
going negotiations on the World Trade Organisation (WTO) Agreement on 
Agriculture, the European Communities (EC) favour a more gradual 
reduction in export subsidies than that  being sought by major agricultural 
products' exporting countries, and also by developing countries like India. 
They have, moreover, linked their flexibility on support and protection in 
the farm sector with incorporation of  non-trade concerns, such as animal 
welfare and food safety, in the negotiations. The EC continues to maintain 
that disciplines on trade and investment should be negotiated in the WTO. 
(b) Along with United Nations Conference on Trade and Development 
(UNCTAD), India had co-sponsored a meeting of like-minded developing 
62 

[18 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
countries on ?.5 June, 2003 at Nyon near Geneva to discuss issues of 
common interest. The issues discuss ed in this meeting were Special 
Products, new Special Safeguard Mechanism for developing countries, 
domestic support modalities for developed countries in order to better 
address the distortions in world agriculture markets, and use of sanitary 
and phyto-sanitary measures to deny market access to developing 
countries. 
(c) Government's priority in these negotiations is to safeguard the 
interests of the Indian farmers, inter alia, by providing appropriate levels 
of tariff protection on imports and taking into account our food security 
and livelihood concerns and increased market access for agricultural 
products of export interest to us. 
(d) India has been building coalitions with other WTO Members holding 
similar interests and concerns. The negotiations are scheduled to be 
concluded by 1 January, 2005.

TB Deaths in Orissa 
2747. MS PRAMILA BOHIDAR: will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that TB is one of the biggest killers in Orissa; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that  the State reports  around 80,000 cases 
of TB annually; 
 
(c) whether the new system, Directly Observed Treatment 
short course (DOT) is playing miracle in controlling this 
menace; and 
(d) to what extent it has been implemented in Orissa and 
the other States of country and proved successful? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) and (b) TB is one of the biggest 
killers in India. About 35,000 TB ca ses are detected and put on treatment 
under the programme annually in the state of Orissa. 
(c) DOTS is very effective in controlling TB. Cure rate is 86% in Orissa 
as against 85% at national level. 
(d) With a view to achieveing a cure rate of 85% of new sputum cases 
and to detect atleast 70% of such cases, the Revised National TB Control 
106 

[18 August. 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Programme (RNTCP) which is a WHO recommended DOTS strategy is 
being implemented in the country in a phased manner since 1997. Till 
date 700 million population of  the country has already been covered under 
the revised strategy. It is envisaged to cover 850 million populations under 
the revised strategy by 2004 and the entire population by 2005. 
The project districts are reporting  treatment success rate of more 
than 80% which means that more than 8 out of every 10 patients detected 
and put on treatment on the revised strategy are successfully treated as 
against less than 4 in the earlier programme. 
In Orissa, out of 30 districts, DOTS strategy is being implemented in 
the 16 tribal districts. The remaining 14 districts are undergoing preparatory 
activities for adoption of revised strategy. 
High Blood Pressure among kids 
2748. SHRI RAJU PARMAR : will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state : 
(a) whether Government are aware on incidence of high blood pressure 
among kids; 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto; 
(c) whether it is a fact that children between the age group of 12-18 
have diseases like high cholesterol, high BP and are under-weight or 
over-weight, besides having other problems; and 
(d) if so, the steps Government have taken or propose to take to 
provide adequate medical facilities to children in the country, and how 
much grant Government are receiving per annum from the World Health 
Organisation and UNICEF? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI 
SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) to (c) According to a published epidemiologica 1 
study of blood pressure in school children (5-14 years) in Delhi, the 
prevalence of Hypertension among school children was around 12% in 
boys and 11.4% in girls. The study covered both Government and Public 
Schools and included all social economic groups. 
As per the ICMR funded study c onducted on adolescents belonging 
to affluent families, high systolic blood pressure among children was found 
in about 30% and high diastolic blood pressure was found 16.7% children 
in the age group of 13-18 years of 5 South Delhi Public Schools. As per 
107 

RAJYA SABHA [ 18 August, 2003 ] 
the study in a sample of 773 children, high cholresterol was observed in 
5.8% children in the age group of 13-18  years of five public schools of 
South Delhi. The percentage of over weight children was about 15% and 
the percentage of the under weight ch ildren was 30.5% in the same group. 
The studies require detailed analysis before coming to a conclusion. 
(d) Providing medicine for needy including children is the responsibility 
of the State Government. However, Central Government supplements the 
efforts of the State Governments by pr oviding medicine/grants etc. through 
various schemes and programmes devis ed for the purpose. Hypertension 
is a condition associated with life-style factors and obesity among children. 
Obesity is generally caused by excessive food intake, improper eating 
habits and lack of physical activity. Education of children to be physically 
active and follow balanced diets are important steps towards prevention 
and management of this disorder.

(c) the number of private medical co lleges in Bihar and the status

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI 
SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) and (b) The upper limit of fee chargeable from 
the students in the Private Unaided  Medical Colleges admitted against 
the 'tree" and "payment" category of seats was being determined by the 
Central Government as per the schme evolved by the Hon'ble Supreme 
Court of India in the Unnikrishnan's case. The scheme evolved in the 
Unnikrisnan's case with regard to admission of students and fixation 
fees has since been overruled by a Constitution Bench of eleven judges 
of the Hon'ble Supreme Court, in its judgement delivered on 31 st October, 
2002 in theT.M.A. Pai Foundation & Ors. Vs. State of Karnataka & Ors., 
wherein inter-alia, it has been held that the unaided private institutions 
shall have the freedom to fix its own free structure. It may generate a 
reasonable surplus which must be used for the betterment and growth of 
the educational institution. However,  it should adopted a rational fee 
structure and would not be entitled to charge capitation fee or indulge in 
profiteeing. 
In the light of the judgement dat ed 31-10-2002 in order to prevent 
over-charging or profiteering by the private unaided medical/dental colleges, 
the Central Government issued broad policy guidelines on 14-5-2003 to 
the State Governments and the Univ ersities and some of the State 
Governments also framed regulations in this regard. On the other hand, 
some of the private unaided institutions claimed complete autonomy as 
regards determination of their own f ee structure and that so long as there 
was no profiteering or charging of capitation fee by them there could be no 
interferece by the Government. The validity of the guidelines dated 14-5-2003 
issued by the Central Government and also the regulations framed by 
some of the State Governments was chalenged by various private medical 
colleges. 
All such petitions were together heard by a Five Judge constitution 
Bench of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India which has delivered its

Professional blood donors 
2756. SHRI MOTILAL VORA : Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state : 
(a) whether Government are aware that professional blood donors 
are donating blood in various hospitals in Delhi by posing themselves as 
relatives of the patients; 
(b) if so, to what exient it is correct; and 
(c) whether Government propose any concrete steps to check this 
and if so, by when? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SMT. 
SUSHMA SWARAJ) : (a) to (c) Professional blood donation has been 
banned with effect from 1 -1 -1998. All the blood banks have been instructed 
by the Drugs Control authority to be  extremely vigilant while screening 
blood donors to ensure that no profe ssional donor is able to donate blood 
as a replacement/relative donor. Under the amended Drugs and Cosmetics 
Rules, it is clearly provided that while screening blood donors, it is to be 
ensured by the blood bank that the arms and forearms of the blood donors 
shall be free from skin punctures or scar indicative of professional blood 
donors. The donor questionnaire also helps in screening out potential 
professional blood donors. Thus a prof essional donor can be identified at 
the stage of screening before blood donation by the attending medical 
officer/staff of the blood bank.

Indications for use of ultrasonography for the well being of Pregnant 
Woman 
(I) Ultrasound is not indicated/ advised/performed to determine the 
sex of foetus except for diagnosis of sex-linked diseases such 
as Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy, Haemophilia A & B etc. 
(ii) During pregnancy Ultrasonography should only be performed 
when indicated. The following is the representative list of 
indications for ultrasound during pregnancy. 
(1) To diagnose intra-uterine and/or ectopic pregnancy and confirm 
viability. 
(2) Estimation of gestational age (dating). 
(3) Detection of number of foetuses and their chorionicity. 
(4) Suspected pregnancy with IUCD in-situ or suspected pregnancy 
following contraceptive failure/MTP failure. 
(5) Vaginal bleeding/leaking. 
(6) Follow-up of cases of abortion. 
(7) Assessment of cervical canal and diameter of internal os. 
(8) Discrepancy between uterine size and period of amenorrhoea. 
(9) Any suspected adenexal or uterine pathalogoy/abnormamy. 
(10) Detection of chromosomal abnorma lities, foetal st ructural defects 
and other abnormalities and their follow-up. 
(11) To evaluate foetal presentaton and position. 
(12) Assessment of liquor amnii. 
(13) Preterm labour/preterm premature rupture of membranes. 
(14) Evaluation of placental position, thickness, grading and 
abnormalities (placenta praevia, retroplacental haemorrhage, 
abnormal adherence etc.). 
(15) Evaluation of umbilical cord -presentation, insertion, nuchal 
encirclement, number of vessels ad presence of true knot. 
144 

[ 18 August, 2003 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(16) Evaluation of previous Caesarean Section scars. 
(17) Evaluation of foetal growth parameters, foetal weight and foetal 
well being. 
(18) Colour flow mapping and duplex Doppler studies. 
(19) Ultrasound guided procedures such as medical terminaton of 
pregnancy, external caphalic versions etc. and their follow-up. 
(20) Adjunct to diagnostic and thereapeutic invasive interventions 
such as chorionic villus smapling (CVS), amniocenteses, foetal 
blood sampling, foetal skin biopsy, amnio-infusion, intrauterine 
infusion, placement of shunts etc. 
(21) Observation of intra-partum events. 
(22) Medical/surgical conditions complicating pregnancy. 
(23) Research/scientific studies in  recognised institutions. Person 
conducting ultrasonography on a pregnant women shall keep 
complete record thereof in the clinic/centre in Form F and any 
deficiency or inaccuracy found therein shall amount to 
contravention of provisions of se ction 5 or section 6 of the Act, 
unless contrary is proved by the person conducting such 
ultrasonography

 female foeticide;

was brought into operation from 1 -1  -1996. The Act prohibits determinatbn 
and disclosure of the sex of foetus . The Act has since been amended

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LAW AND 
JUSTICE (SHRI P.C. THOMAS): (a) The scheme of Fast Track Courts 
(FTC) was introduced in the year 2001 on the recommendation of the 
Eleventh Finance Commission. Its main aim and objective is to dispose 
of long pending Sessions cases (pending for two or more years) and 
cases of under-trial prisoners who are languishing in jail for years. The 
Eleventh Finance Commission fixed a target of 1734 Fast Track Courts 
to be set up over a period of five years (from the year 2001-2005). 
(b) Since its inception the scheme has been found to be effective in 
quick disposal of cases. As on 31st July, 2003. 1.74.715 cases have 
been disposed of by Fast Track Courts out of 3.26,059 cases which were 
transferred to such FTCs. Out of the target of 1734 FTCs, 1356 have 
been notified and 1074 are functional as on 31st July, 2003.

not set up all the FTCs in their State due to non-availability of suitable

required manpower to man these FTCs. The Central Government have 
advised such State Governments to take available buildings on rent and 
recruit qualified and eligible persons from the Bar for appointment as 
Judges so that all the FTCs could be established and made functional as 
per the target fixed.

Agreement of Vadinar Port 
2816. SHRIMATI SAVITA SHARDA: 
SHRI LALITBHAI MEHTA: 
Will the Minister of SHIPPING be pleased to state : 
 (a) whether it is a  fact that an agreement was signed and approved 
vide Government of India's letter dated 10th October, 1977 between the 
177 

RAJYA SABHA [18 August, 2003] 
Government of Gujarat and the Central Government that Vadinar would 
be an oil import terminal for Indian Oil Corporation only; 
(b) whether it is a fact that Kandia Port Trust has granted permission 
to put a SBM and Jetties to Essar Oil Ltd. at Vadinar; 
(c) if so, whether it is not a clear violation of the agreement entered 
into on the 10th October, 1977; and 
(d) Government's views regarding handling over of Vadinar port to 
the State Government of Gujarat? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SHIPPING (SHRI 
DILIPKUMAR MANSUKHLAL GANDHI): (a) No, Sir. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) Does not arise in view of reply to part (a) above. 
(d) Vadinar was included in the limit of Kandia Port after Government 
of Gujarat issued notification deleting it from the limit of Minor Port of 
Salaya, while the Government of India issued notification for its inclusion 
in the limit of Kandia Major Port. Go vernment of Gujarat, from time to 
time, has been requesting to revert Vadinar, by de-linking it from Kandia 
Port limit. By the said notifications  issued by both the Governments, 
i.e., Government of India and Government of Gujarat, Kandia Port Trust 
has been vested with the jurisdiction of Vadinar Port and, thus, is under 
the administrative control of the Board of Trustees of the Port of Kandia. 
Since the Vadinar is an integral part of the Kandia Port Trust and its 
development has to be undertaken by Kandia Port Trust, the request of 
Government of Gujarat to hand over t he Vadinar Port to State Government 
cannot be agreed to. However, Government of India had offered to 
Government of Gujarat for forming a joint venture company with Kandia 
Port and the Gujara t Maritime Board as partners for the development of 
Vadinar for multi-purpose use.

belonging to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes is implemented by

Statement of Facts 
No formal Committees as such were formed by Government in 1991, 
1996 and 2000 for strengthening of the Government of India Stationery 
office, Kolkata. However, a resolution was issued by the Government on 
27-2-1991 revoking the earlier resolution of 16-10-87 winding up the GISO, 
Kolkata. The resolution also ordered to  make a study to establish whether 
there has been any economy in the pur chase of stationery items after 
issue of the orders regarding winding up of GISO on 16-10- 87. In the year 
1996, the Government entrusted the work of study on the organisational 
aspect of GISO, Kolkata to the Depar tment of Administrative Reforms 
and Public Grievances and that Depa rtment submitted its report in 
October, 1997. The study made the re commendation that either the GISO 
should be converted into an autonomous organisation or that the Internal 
work Study Unit of this Ministry sh ould undertake the staff assessment 
study. The Ministry decided to acc ept the second alternative and the 
Internal work Study Unit was assigned the job of making assessment of 
staff requirement of GISO along with its 3 regional depots. The Internal 
work Study Unit of the Ministry gave its recommendations in the year 
2000 recommending continuation of this organization with reduced staff 
strength. This recommendation has been accepted by this Ministry and 
the matter has to be taken to the committee of Secretaries as this 
recommendation is at variance with the recommendations of the 
Expenditure Reforms Commission who recommended closure of this 
Organization.

Dual pipeline system for Dwarka 
2848. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHA RJEE: Will the Minister of 
URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to 
state : 
(a) whether the Delhi Development Au thority is installing dual pipeline 
system for Dwarka sub city flats; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether it is a fact that ther e is acute shortage of sweet water 
used for drinking purpose in Dwarka; 
(d) if so, the steps to augment the supply of water in the area; and 
(e) The steps proposed to be taken to ensure that no mixing of water 
to be supplied takes place in the two type of pipes? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI PON 
RADHAKRISHNAN): (a) and (b) The Delhi Development Authority has 
reported that dual pipeline system in the new houses in Dwarka Sub-city 
is being installed since Delhi Jal Board is not able to meet 100% 
requirement of water on account of non-release of raw water by the 
neighbouring States of Haryana and U.P.The water for drinking and cooking 
purposes will be supplied only in the kitchen while water for flushing, 
washing and other aomestic purposes w ill be supplied in WC & bathroom 
through overhead tanks from tube-well sources. 
212 

[ 18 August, 2003 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) and (d) Delhi Jal Board (D JB) has reported that they are supplying 
2.5 to 3 Million Gallons per day (MGD) for Dwarka area from its 40 MG D 
Nangloi Water Treatment Plant which is  functioning at half the capacity 
on account of non-availability of raw water from Haryana. To augment the 
supply of water in Dwarka area, Delhi Jal Board has a long term plan to 
set up 40 MGD Water Treatment Plant at Dwarka for which DDA has 
identified the land. Raw water for this plant will be available from the 
saving of seepage losses of water afte r the construction of parallel car.a! 
channel from Munak to Haiderpur for which the work has been taKen in 
hand. The construction of channel will  take about 3 years. Rain water 
harvesting and recharging of acquiter/ ground water source are also being 
undertaken with a view ;to augment the water supply from tube wells. 
(e) The DDA proposes to construct separate reservoirs for drinking 
and domestic use of water. Water is proposed to be supplied by two 
separate lines having different colour codes so that there is no mix-up.

Ichampalli and Polavaram irrigation projects 
*382. DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY:  Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have received any request from the 
Government of Andhra Pradesh to execute major irrigation projects such 
as Ichampalli and Polavaram; 
(b) if so, whether Government propose to take them up for execution; 
and 
(c) by when they are likely to be completed? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RE SOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
1 
 

RAJYA SABHA [19 August, 2003] 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Yes, sir. The Hon'ble Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh in 
January, 2001 had requested the Central Government for declaring 
Inchampalli and Pollavaram Projects as National Projects and their 
implementation by the Union Government. After examining the request, 
the Hon'ble Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh was informed in February, 
2001 that there was no proposal to treat any such river valley project in 
the country as a National Project. 
Irrigation being a State subject, the responsibility of planning, 
investigation, funding along with priority execution, operation and 
maintenance of irrigation projects, including irrigation and flood control 
Projects primarily rests with the con cerned State Government themselves. 
Inchampalli and Pollavaram Projects involve inter-State aspects and their 
completion depend upon the resolution of inter-State issues between the 
riparian States. 
DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY: Sir, the hon. Minister has, in his reply, 
stated that Ichamapalli and Polavaram projects in Andhra Pradesh cannot 
be taken up as National Projects as ' Irrigation' is a Stat e Subject., Sir, I 
would like to know why the Government of India couldn't declare Ichampalli 
and Polavaram Projects as National Projects when the Damodar Valley 
Project, catering only to the State of West Bengal, had been declared as 
a National Project. 
SHRI ARJUN CHARAN SETHI: Sir, the first step in the implementation 
of such a project is its clearance by the Central Water Commission; then, 
there has to be the investment clearance. There are so many processes 
involved before any project is taken up for implementation. Ichampalli 
and Polavaram projects are inter-State  projects. Unless all the States 
involved in the case of Polavaram project, the States of Orissa, Andhra 
Pradesh and Chhattisgarh and, in the case of Ichampalli project, the States 
of Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh and Chhattisgarh - agree on the 
implementation of these projects, these projects cannot be taken up. So, 
the first step is that of an agreem ent between the States, because these 
are all inter-State projects. Unfortunately, for example, Chhattisgarh is 
very much against the implementation of these projects. All the riparian 
States are not agreeable on the implementation of these projects. So, at 
this juncture, these cannot be considered.

†*383. SHRI ABHAY KANT PRASAD: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have reviewed the irrigation works in tribal

THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
Be Answered on 19.08.2003 Regarding Funds for Irrigation Projects 
in Tribal Areas. 
(a) to (c) Yes, Sir. There are 73 major and 114 medium ongoing irrigation 
projects in the X Five Year Plan wh ich are benefiting tribal areas of 16 
States. The ultimate irrigation potential of these 187 major and medium 
projects is 11.27 mha. and the achieveme nt of potential upto IX Plan is 
4.13 mha. 
(d) Special efforts have been initiated by the Government for 
development of irrigation in tribal areas according to the revised National 
Water Policy, 2002 which stipulates "special efforts should be made to 
investigate and formulate projects eith er in, or for the benefit of, areas 
inhabited by tribal or other specially disadvantaged groups such as socially 
weak, scheduled castes and scheduled tribes."

The Union Planning Commission has identified actionable points for 
development Water Sector wherein following targets had been made which 
also include projects of Tribal areas: 
1. To complete 30 major projects of Pre-fifth and Fifth Plan period 
by the States. 
2. To complete 20 major and medium projects under Fast Track of 
Accelerated Irrigation Benefit Progr amme (AIBP) for creation of 
additional 0.475 mha of irrigation potential. 
3. To create an additional 3 mha of irrigation potential through normal 
AIBP projects/schemes. 
Further, at present, out of 69 New project proposals benefiting the 
tribal areas (Under Tribal Sub Plan) there are 39 projects under different 
stages of appraisal in Central Water Commission, 29 have been techno- 
economically accepted by the Advisory Committee of the Ministry of Water 
Resources and one project has b een recommended to Planning 
Commission for investment clearance. 
(e) The allocation of funds for irrigation development in tribal areas is 
done by the concerned State Governments out of their overall allocation. 
The overall allocation for the irrigation projects including projects in the 
tribal areas for State Government of Jharkhand for the X. Five Year Plan is 
Rs. 14.632.74 crore white the agreed only for the Annual Plans 2002-03 
and 2003-04 is Rs. 2652.00 crore and Rs. 2935.85 crore respectively.

SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: Mr. Chairman, Sir, I would 
like to know from the hon. Minister whether it is not true that the Indian 
exporters are struggling to improve their competitive edge in terms of 
price as their counterparts in China, who are getting credit at the rate of 
5 per cent, in Japan, the exporters are getting credit at the rate of 0.07 per 
cent and the US exporters are getting at the rate of 1.5 per cent whereas 
the Indian exporters are getting loans for exporting goods at the rate of 
8 to 13 per cent of interest. Does this rate of interest on credit not hamper 
our exports? So, what steps the Ministry is proposed to take to reduce 
the rate of interest on credit for our exports and bring it at per with that of 
the other countries mentioned above? 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Mr. Chairman, Sir, if I understand the thrust 
of the hon. Member's question, it is that in comparison to other countries, 
firstly, our exporters suffer from a de bility of having to borrow at a higher 
rate of interest and therefore, his suggestion is that we should make 
export credit available on easier terms.  If I have understood that correctly, 
Sir, this is what I would say in answer. Sir, the whole question of interest 
rates is a complex question. Whereas industries, manufacturers, legitimately 
and understandably, would want a lower interest regime so that they are 
able to access credit at a competitiv ely lower price, citizens and the 
saving public would naturally want a higher interest regime so that their 
investments receive and are able to receive suitable returns. It is the 
correct balance that we have to strike  in between these,  taking into account 
also the prevailing international interest regime. So it is not possible that 
India be an island of peculiar interest regime outside of what the global 
trends are. So far as export credit a nd the interest rate on export credit 
are concerned, we have to follow the stipulation of PLR minus 2, which is 
the guideline at the present moment. The minute we deviate from it, we 
will in fact, be inviting the WTO restrictions on the subject. So, we cannot 
be promoting exports through subsidised interest rates and that is the 
difficulty.

Task force on infrastructure 
2870. SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION 
be pleased to state : 
(a) whether upgradation of major metro airports in India to world class 
standards was one of the mandates given by the Task Force on 
Infrastructure, set up by the Prime Minister in 1998; and 
(b) if so, the details of progress made by the Ministry of Civil Aviation 
from 1998 till date in this respect? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDY): (a) Yes Sir. 
(b) The Task Force on Infrastructure on 9.12.1998 recommended that 
airports at Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore be corporatised. Based on this 
recommendation, Government of India in January, 1999 decided to 
corporatise the airports at Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata, besides 
construction of Greenfield Airport at Bangalore. Considering the 
compIexities involved in corporatisation, the Task Force on 3.6.1999 
approved the leasing route. Government of India in January, 2000 approved 
restructuring of airports of Airports Authority of India through long term 
leasing route as and when found suitable. The airports at Delhi, Mumbai 
Kolkota and Chennai were taken up for this exercise at the first instance. 
The Financial Consultant and Legal Consultant for restructuring exercise 
were appointed in March, 2000 and March, 2001 respectively. An Inter- 
Ministerial Group (IMG) was constituted to advise and monitor the entire 
exercise. The IMG met periodically to  discuss and deliberate on various 
strategic issues. Pre-lnvestment Meets were held in New Delhi and London 
in April, 2002 to formally introduce the long term lease process. The Meet 
was attended by many Airport Operators, Financial Companies etc. An 
Amendment Bill was introduced in the Parliament on 30.11.2000 for 
54 

[19 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
incorporating and enabling provision in the Airports Authority of India (AAI) 
Act, 1994 providing for leasing of ai rports. The Bill was referred to the 
Department Related Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and 
Culture. The Committee tabled its report on 21.11.2002. As per the 
recommendations of the Committee, a comprehensive Airports Authority 
of India (Amendment) Bill, 2003 was introduced in the Parliament.The Bill 
as passed by Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha on 9.5.2003 and 28.7.2003 
respectively. Meanwhile, the restructuring through Joint Venture route was 
also considered. The Hon'ble Finance Minister in Budget Speech 2003-04 
has inter alia announced that in addition to the existing initiatives for 
leasing of major airports, the Delhi and Mumbai airports will be taken up 
for modernisation to international standards through formation of two Joint 
Venture companies. Steps have been taken for incorporation of two 
separate companies for Delhi and Mumbai airports. The transaction 
structure is being finalised in consultation with Ministry of Finance.

(c) The terms and conditions prescribed for loans vary from institution 
to institution and are set out briefly below: 
SIDBI provides assistance to small scale units through indirect and 
direct finance schemes.The norms under the refinance (indirect) schemes 
are generally prescribed by the Prim ary Lending Institutions concerned. 
As regards directs assistance schemes of SIDBI for small scale units 
such as Project Finance Scheme (PFS), generally, debt equity ratio (DER)

not exceeding 2 :1 is applicable. Re payment period and moratorium is 
fixed taking into account the debt servicing capacity of the borrowing unit 
in respect of Equipment Finance Scheme (EFS), the DER is generally 
note more than 2 :1 for the project and 1.5 :1 for the company, as a 
whole. As regards special schemes such as Technology Development 
and Modernisation Fund Scheme (TDMFS), the lending norms/terms are 
relatively more liberal. As regards norms/parameters, a flexible approach 
is adopted and decisions are taken based on the overall assessment of 
the project. 
ICICI Bank Ltd. The Interest rate a pplicable to financial assistance 
for the projects is specified depending on the rating assigned based on 
Internal risk perception of the project s. The stipulated security package 
includes mortgage on fixed assets on the project and in specific cases, 
personal guarantee(s) from the promoters. The repayment schedule is 
fixed based on projected cash flows out of the project and usually 
commences after envisaged commissioni ng of the project and start of 
commercial operations. To ensure fiscal discipline in project 
commissioning, disbursements are usually made depending on 
achievement of specific project related milestones and only after means 
of finance is tied up. The progress of the project is monitored through 
periodic site visits, discussion with promoters, scrutiny of project 
documents and certifications by competent authorities. 
EXIM Bank offers export credit facilities to facilitate exports on deferred 
payment terms, apart from supporting overseas construciton, consultancy 
and turnkey projects. 
IFCI insists on securities, like pa ri-passu charge on fixed assets, 
personal guarantee, pledge of shares, first charge on fixed assets, etc. 
IDBI while extending loans to industrial projects, IDBI stipulate certain

creation, personal and corporate gu arantees, etc. to ensure timely 
implementation of the projects within the estimated cost and to enable 
the lenders to closely monitor the projects duri ng the pendency of 
assistance.

Report of Banchu Committee of black money 
†2900. SHRI ISAM SINGH: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether the Banchu Committee has published its report with 
reference to origin of black money in the country from 1960 to 1980; and 
(b) if so, the measures Government propose to take to check it? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) The Direct Taxes Enquiry 
Committee (Wanchoo Committee) in it s final Report of December, 1971 
estimated black income at Rs. 700 crores for the year 1961 -62, Rs. 1000 
crores for the year 1965-66 and Rs.-1800 crores for the year 1968-69. 
 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
 81 

RAJYA SABHA [19 August, 2003] 
(b) Necessary legislative, fiscal  and administrative measures are 
continuously taken to prevent the ge neration and flow of black money. 
Rates of taxation have been progressi vely rationalized. Various provisions 
in the Income Tax Act; like compulsory maintenance/audit of accounts in 
appropriate cases unde r section 44AA/44AB, restrictions on cash 
transactions under section 40A(3), 269SS, 269T and penalties/prosecutions 
for punishing tax defaulters, are aimed at preventing generation and flow 
of black money. Searches and su rveys in appropriate cases are 
continuously undertaken to unearth the black money. General information 
is also gathered by the Central Info rmation Branches of the Income Tax 
Department about various financial transactions. Simplification of 
procedures for filing returns and for making payment of taxes are also 
directed towards greater compliance by the tax payers, which will be an 
anti-dote to tax evasion.

Law for water harvesting 
3005. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to enact a law not to allow building 
of individual homes or housing societies without water harvesting provisions 
throughout the country; 
(b) if so, by when an enactment is anticipated; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; 
(d) the targets fixed by Government to augment the water availability 
by reviving the traditional water system and by constructing the water 
harvesting structures throughout the country; and 
(e) the achievement made so far through both the ways? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (c) The Union 
Government do not propose to enact a law not to allow building of individual 
homes or housing societies without water harvesting provisions throughout 
the country due to the following reasons:— 
(1) Under the Constitution of India 'Water' is a State subject and, 
thererfore, any legislation in the matter can be considered only 
by the State Legislatures. However, the Ministry of Water 
Resources has advised the Ministry of Urban Development and 
Poverty Alleviation to make roof top rain water harvesting 
mandatory. Accordingly, the Ministry of Urban Development & 
Poverty Alleviation has amended Building Bye-laws, 1983 making 
provision for water harvesting through storing of water run-off 
including rain water in all new buildings on plots of 100 square 
meters and above in Delhi mandatory. Besides, the State 
Governments of Haryana and Tamil Nadu have also issued 
amendments to municipal building bye-laws to make roof top 
rain water harvesting mandatory for specified category of 
buildings. The Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA) constituted 
under Section 3 (3) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 
has also issued directions to group housing societies, institutions, 
schools, hotels, industrial establishments and farm houses 
 161 

RAJYA SABHA [19 August. 2003] 
located in 'notified areas' of South and South West districts of 
NCT Delhi, Municipal Corporation of Faridabad and Ballabgarh of 
Haryana, Municipal Corporation of  Ghaziabad in Uttar Pradesh, 
GurgaonTown and adjoining Industrial Areas of Gurgaon district 
of Haryana to adopt roof top rain water harvesting systems. The 
CGWA has also issued directions to all group housing societies 
in NCT of Delhi located in areas where ground water levels are 
more than 8 metres and are abst racting ground water to adopt 
roof top rain water harvesting system. 
(2) Water harvesting is not required in all areas of the country. There 
are areas having excess rainfall and ground water level very 
shallow. In some of the areas, even the problem of water logging 
is prevalent. 
(3) The objective can be achieved by creating mass awareness and 
organising training programmes etc. The Central Ground water 
Board (CGWB) under the Ministry of Water Resources, has 
already conducted 135 mass awareness programmes and 69 
training programmes throughout the country. 
(d) and (e) 'Water' being a State subject, it is primarily the responsibility 
of the concerned State Governments to  plan, finance and execute schemes 
to augment ground water resources. However, during the ninth Plan, the 
Central Ground water Board (CGWB) has implemented a Central Sector 
Scheme on "Studies on Recharge to Ground Water" under which 174 artificial 
recharge schemes have been approved in 27 States and U.Ts. across the 
country. All these schemes are being implemented as per targets and 115 
schemes have been completed so far. The completed schemes have 
shown positive impact in terms of rise in ground water level. However, no 
scheme to augment the water availability by reviving the traditional water 
system was undertaken under the above scheme. Further, with a view to 
augment ground water resources, the Central Government has formulated 
a Centrally Sponsored Scheme on "Ar tificial Recharge to Groundwater 
and Rain Water Harvesting" at an es timated cost of Rs.175 crore for 
implementation during the Tenth Plan. Under the Scheme, construction of 
water harvesting structures including revival of traditional water systems 
are envisaged. The scheme is at consultation stage.

SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, the Regional 
Rural Banks were established in 1975, essentially, for taking banking to 
the doorsteps of the rural masses particularly in areas without banking 
facilities. The Central Government is  the largest shareholder with 50 per

major commercial bank which holds 35 pe r cent of the share capital of the 
RRBs. Presently, there are 196 RRBs spread over 476 districts with a

priority sectors which account for 70 per cent of the total advances,

against the estimated loss of income of Rs. 2,500 crores for the entire 
banking sector. This is more than the combined profit of all the RRBs, and 
unless the Central Government, which is the largest shareholder, does 
something urgently to make up for the possible loss to RRBs, there is a 
threat of their closure, denying banking to a large section of rural India. I 
rquest the Government to come out with measures to help the RRBs.

the RRBs so that it can serve the farming community better. Thank you.

granting statehood to Delhi had been prepared by the Union Home Ministry 
and approved by the Cabinet. The Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha 
yesterday. But the long-pending demand of t he Union Territory of Pondicherry 
has not been considered by the Government. 
Sir, different Governments of Pondicherry have been requesting the 
Government of India for granting Statehood to the Union Territory of 
Pondicherry. Unanimous Resolutions have been passed in this respect. 
When the D.M.K. party was in power, a Resolution had been passed 
unanimously in the Assembly demanding Statehood for Pondicherry. All 
the Members of the legislature, the political leaders and the Members of 
Parliament met the Home Minister in this regard. But their demand has 
not been accepted. 
Sir, the elected representatives are facing administrative difficulties 
since the powers of the Chief Minister  and other Ministers are limited. All 
matters have to be referred to the Home  Ministry and the Lt. Governor for 
approval. Several proposals are either rejected, or, delayed because of 
this requirement of reference to the Home Ministry and the Lt. Governor. 
The feelings of public represent ataives have not been taken into 
consideration. 
So, the Government of India should grant Statehood and also the 
'Special Category' status to the Union Territory of Pondicherry.

has given more than 22.5 lakh LPG gas connections to BPL women in 
Andhra Pradesh. The objective of this scheme is to provide relief to the 
BPL women from drudgery in cooking with firewood, to protect the

Government of Andhra Pradesh has decided to give them a helping hand

Urgent need for rationalisation of 
Crop Insurance Scheme 
SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA (Andhra Pradesh): Madam Deputy Chairman, 
the National Agricultural Insurance Scheme was introduced in 1999 for 
protecting the farmers against losses suffered by them due to natural 
calamities. The Government is taking a Mandal as a unit. The NAIS 
envisages, premium, for cereals, puls es, etc., at 2.5 per cent, oilseeds 
3.5 per cent and for commercial crops 6.55 per cent. To implement this, 
the Government of India set up the Agricultural Insurance Organisation. 
The AIO is adopting various methods to find out losses incurred by farmers, 
but without much help to them. For hi gh risk, indemnity is given at 60 per 
cent, for medium 80 per cent and for low-risk 90 per cent. To calculate 
loss, the AIO is putting threshold limit by taking average production of the 
last five years. Even in this, the AIO is adopting different methods for 
different crops. For example, rice or wheat taking threshold limit of last 
three years and for other crops, threshold limit is five years, and calculates 
204 

[19 August. 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
it with current year's production. If the current year's production is less 
than the average threshold limit, only then farmers get compensation. 
Secondly, groundnut was in medium-risk list in 1999, but later it included 
in high-risk list, and compensation was reduced to 60 per cent from 80 per 
cent, premium was increased to 3.5 per cent and subsidy given by the 
Government to farmers was reduced to 30 per cent from 50 per cent. This 
is only an iota of the problems. So, I request the Government of India to 
rationalise the NAIS and take a village as a unit. While calculating for 
payment of compensation, the Governm ent of India must take two years 
average crop rather than five years to decide the threshold limit. I also 
request that the activities of the AIO should be extended to Mandal level 
for effective implementation of the scheme. Thank you, Madam.

Licences granted for operation of Basic Service in 1997-1998 to six

balance VPTs by the end of 2003 after excluding the categories 
of villages identified as de-populated villages, villages with 
population less than 100, Naxalite or insurgency affected villages 
and to be covered by satellite media in the first phase, failing 
which steps for encashment of the Performance Bank Guarantee 
will be initiated. The fulfilment of the commitments given by the 
Private Basic Service Operators is closely monitored and 
Performance Bank Guarantee would be liable to be encashed in 
case of failure. 
(iii) BSNL has planned to provide 11063 VPTs using Wireless in 
Local Loop (WLL) technology during 2003-2004. The balance 
18006 VPTs will be set up via Satellite media subject to availability 
of funds. 
(iv) The Bill to establish Universal Service Obligatbn Fund has been 
introduced in the Lok Sabha. It is proposed to provide support to 
the various Service Providers for maintenance of VPTs and 
replacement of MARR based VPTs, from this Fund.

*418. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether slippage in implementation of major infrastructure projects 
like roads, railways and power has resulted in cost escalation of projects; 
(b) if so, the percentage of escalation in cost as originally envisaged; 
(c) whether these projects have also been delayed; and 
(d) the steps taken or proposed to be taken to check the escalation 
of cost and expedite the completion of projects? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STATISTICS AND 
PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION (SHRI SATYABRATA 
MOOKHERJEE): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The percentage of cost escalation with respect to 
the original approved cost in respect of major projects costing Rs. 100 
crore and above in roads, railways and power sectors are 3,54.5 and 35 
respectively. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. The steps taken to check the escalation of cost 
and complete the projects within schedule are as follows: 
(i)   Adoption of two- stage clearance system a nd stricter appraisal 
of project reports before investment approval; 
(ii)   Taking up of projects for implementation only after funds have 
been fully tied up; 
(iii) In-depth review of projects on monthly as well as quarterly basis 
by the Government; 
(iv) Follow up with the State Governments in respect of problems 
relating to acquisition of land, re habilitation related issues, forest 
clearances, provision of infrastruc ture facilities and ensuring law 
and order at project sites, etc. 
(v) Setting up of ah Empowered Committee in the administrative 
Ministries for review of departmentally executed projects;

(vii) Setting up of Standing Committees in the Ministries/Departments 
to fix responsibility for time and cost overruns; 
(viii) Appointment of nodal officers fo r each project with continuity of 
tenure; and 
(ix)   Issue of guidelines on standard bidding documents for adoption.

Traditional wireline solutions are increasingly supplemented by 
wireless technologies for providing connectivity in remote villages because 
of the number of advantages such as  maintainability etc. These include 
point to point Very High Frequency/Ultra High Frequency (VHF/UHF) Radio, 
Multi Access Rural Radio System (MARRS), Digital Enhanced Cordless 
Telecommunications (CorDECT), Code Division Multiple Access (CDMA) 
based WLL, INMARSAT, etc. 
Technology based on IEEE 802.11b/a/g standards hold promise for 
high bandwidth connection in the future. For this DIT has been carrying 
out a project called "Digital Gangetic Plains" implemented by IIT Kanpur 
to test out the viability of this techno logy for rural connection. The project 
aims to use the technology based on 802.11 b IEEE Standard working in 
the 2.4 GHz to 2.4835 GHz for providing wireless connectivity to villages 
in the corridor between Lucknow and Kanpur. Data up to a few Mbps 
throughput had been obtained through the wireless link and potential for 
setting up of rural information kiosks look promising, though economies 
are yet to be established.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SUBHASH 
MAHARIA): (a) and (b) Foodgrains of fair average quality conforming to  
 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
101 

RAJYA SABHA [21 August, 2003] 
the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act (PFA) standards are distributed

Some complaints about the quality of foodgrains supplied under the 
PDS were received during the last three years. 
During 2000-2001, co mplaints were received from the State 
Governments of Arunachal Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir, Karnataka, 
Sikkim and Tripura regarding supply of foodgrains of poor quality, especially 
rice procured under relaxed specifications (URS). Keeping in view the 
reluctance of consumers, the supply  of URS rice of 1997-98 Kharif 
Marketing Season was stopped. 
During 2001-2002, the Governments of Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, 
Maharashtra, Rajasthan and NCT of Delhi complained about the supply 
of "luster lost" wheat while the Government of Goa and Kerala complained 
about the poor quality of rice stocks. It was explained to the State 
Governments that, except in appearance, lustre lost wheat is as good as 
sound wheat, especially in terms of nutritional value. The FCI officers 
were instructed to ensure that rice of good quality only was supplied 
under the PDS to Goa and Kerala. 
During 2002-03, the Governments of Rajasthan, Delhi, Gujarat and 
Maharashtra had complained about issue of poor quality of "lustre lost" 
wheat under PDS and Government of Karnataka and Kerala had 
complained about the issue of poor quality of rice under various schemes. 
Keeping in view the reluctance of co nsumers, the issue of "luster lost" 
wheat for distribution under TPDS was stopped. FCI was instructed to 
ensure that rice of good quality only is supplied under the PDS in 
Karnataka and Kerala. 
(c) and (d) No, Sir. FCI stores foodgrains in scientifically constructed 
godowns under proper supervision of trained quality control officials who 
preserve the quality of foodgrains during storage. FCI has a standard 
procedure for issuing stocks under the "first in first out" principle. State 
Governments are free to inspect the stocks of foodgrains and satisfy 
themselves about their quality before lifting the same from FCI depots. 
The State Governments have also been advised to depute an officer not 
below the rank of Inspector to check the quality of stocks.

117 

RAJYA SABHA [21 August, 2003] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI V. SREENIVASA 
PRASAD): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. In view  of the Report of Centre for Science 
and Environment (CSE), a Non-Governmental Organization, regarding 
presence of pesticide residues in the Bottled water, the Government had 
constituted an Inquir y Committee under the Chairpersonship of 
Smt. Satwant Reddy, Additional Secretar y in the Department of Consumer 
Affairs on 5th February, 2003. The Committee submitted its Report on 
25th March, 2003. The major findigns and recommendations of the Report 
in respect of functioning of Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) are as per 
Statement (See below,). The Government has accepted all the 
recommendations of the Inquiry Committee pertaining to BIS. 
Statement 
The major findings and recommendations of the 
Reddy Committee report 
* BIS has an established system for developing and formulating 
standards by involving different sector. Consensus is an essential 
procedural principle and a necessa ry condition for the preparation 
of Standards. Further BIS has adopted the International 
Organization for Standardization (ISO) Guide 7—1982 on the 
requirements suitable for product certification. The views 
expressed by the scientists, consumer organization and DGHS 
(PFA) on draft standards are taken into consideration. Overall, 
the prescribed procedure was fo llowed while formulating these 
two standards for Packaged Drinking Water. The BIS Secretariat 
has carried out its assigned function of identifying appropriate 
Sectional Committees, consulting the interested sectors, 
placement of comments before the Sectional Committee, and 
recording of the decisions re lated to each of the quality 
parameters. The standards have specified all those 
characteristics and requirements that are necessary, the required 
limiting values and also the test methods. 
* BIS certification for Packaged Drinking Water and Packaged 
Natural Mineral Water was made mandatory under PFA by Ministry 
of Health and Family Welfare through two Notifications issued on 
29th September, 2000. Before these Notifications were issued, 
118 

[21 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
the matter was discussed by experts in the Central Committee 
for Food Standards (CCFS), set up under Rule 3 of PFA Act. 
This Committee, under the Chairmanship of Director General of 
Health Services considered the BIS standards and found them 
adequate for adoption under PFA. The specifications for 
pesticides residue under PFA standards as well as BIS standards 
are "below detectable limit". 
* The Committee found that the standards for Packaged Drinking 
Water and Packaged Natural Mineral Water were adequate and 
the detection limits of pesticides  residue in these two standards 
compare favourably with pesticide residues in other food items 
such as milk, fruits, vegetabl es and foodgrain s, which account 
for a major portion of daily intake by human beings. For example 
existing test methods detect DDT in packaged water upto the 
level of 0.02 ppm, whereas in milk and milk products (on a fat 
basis), it is permitted upto 1.25 ppm under PFA. 
* The two standards on Packaged Drinking Water were formulated 
by deriving assistance from Codex and WHO guidelines. At that 
time Codex had not yet agreed upon the relevant test method for 
detection and determination of pesticide residues. Hence the 
concerned Technical Committee of BIS decided to adopt the test 
method standard established by another technical committee of 
BIS, which were prescribed for pesticides residues in fruits, 
vegetables and soils. These standard test methods were not 
specifically meant for drinking water. Since an agreed Codex 
test method was not available at that time, no individual officer 
or organization can be held responsible for this weak link in the 
test method adopted. 
* A pro-active approach towards keeping the standards dynamic 
and at par with international developments in related fields is 
necessary. This would ensure that BIS strives for continuous 
improvement of standards by providing for an in-built alert system, 
which would flag emerging problems before they assume 
threatening dimensions. 
* BIS should have a Core Group of Scientists from various fields 
with the responsibility of keeping track of recent scientific and 
119 

RAJYA SABHA [21 August, 2003] 
technical developments in critical areas. These scientists would 
alert the BIS management on the need to update and revise 
particular standards even before the review is due. 
* Draft standards should be put on the Website of BIS in order to 
obtain comments from all interested individuals and groups. This 
should be brought to public notice by giving advertisements in 
the print and electronic media. 
* The standard formulation is a voluntary activity and BIS does 
not pay anything, even in terms of TA/DA, for participation in 
meetings of the Technical Committees set up for standard 
formulation. As a result, at times, scientific organizations and 
consumer organizations are not able to participate in the meetings 
of Technical Committees. There is an  urgent need to take remedial 
measures to get over this problem. 
* The steps involved in the certification process as laid down in 
the BIS Act, Certification Regulations and Manual of Operations 
etc. have been followed in li censing the manufacturing units. 
Surveillance inspections and picking up of samples from the 
factory and the market place for assessing their conformity to 
the requirements of standard in a recognized laboratory have 
also been carried out. Instances of action taken, including 
stoppage of marking when non-compliance was observed, indicate 
that supervision and monitoring, required under the scheme were 
carried out. However, some shortfall was observed in the targets 
set for frequency of surveillance inspections and testing of 
samples. It has also been observed that in addition to the existing 
demands for certification, about 750 licences for Packaged 
Drinking Water were added for which additional resources like 
manpower were not provided. Constraints of manpower available 
for the over all certification and enforcement activities of BIS 
might, therefore, have contributed to the shortfall noiticed in the 
surveillance inspection. No single individual can be held 
responsible for this. 
* When BIS certification for an item of mass consumption like 
packaged water is made mandatory, it increases the responsibility 
and answerability of BIS towards the consumers. BIS should 
120 

[21 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
have a complete in-house review  of its resources before accepting 
this responsibility. Inadequacies of manpower and other resources 
should be identified and ways to fill up those gaps be explored 
before the challenge is accepted. But once BIS has accepted 
this responsibility, it must discharge it faithfully and not cite lack 
of manpower or resources as justification for non-adherence to 
the norms. 
* BIS prepares one Scheme of Testing and Inspection (STI) for 
each product, after due consideration of the specifications in the 
relevant standard but this STI, once prepared beco mes applicable 
to all licensees of that product. In the European directives, it is 
found that the frequency of sampling and analysis for water put 
into bottles or containers for sale varies according to the capacity 
of production. It is suggested that BIS may consider the 
desirability of linking the frequency of testing with the production. 
In other words instead of a single STI for all licensees, BIS may 
take into account the quality of raw water, the technology used 
for purifying and quantity of water produced in a day and develop 
a STI for that individual manufacturing unit. 
* BIS may consider setting up product specific committees, as 
prevailing in AFNOR (French Standard body), having provision 
for outside expert participation at least for certification of 
mandatory items. This will enable BIS to involve the mandating 
body, say PFA of DGHS or its nominee to advise on the STI, 
choice of testing laboratories and overall implementation 
effectiveness of the scheme. 
* In addition to BIS's Central Labo ratory, Sahibabad, services of 
13 other laboratories were made use of by BIS for testing of the 
samples drawn. It was necessary for evaluation of applications 
for grant of licence and for superv ision, the recognition of the - 
laboratories has been based on international standards regarding 
the competence of the testing laboratories. The laboratories have 
followed the testing methods specified in the standard and have 
submitted reports in the time in properly designed format 
indicating the specified value an d the values obtained for the 
samples submitted. 
121 

RAJYA SABHA [21 August, 2003] 
* The Bureau of Indian Standards, the National Standards Body of 
India, became functional as a statutory body under the Bureau 
of Indian Standards Act, 1986 with effect from 1 April, 1987 
taking over the staff, assets and liabilities of Indian Standards 
Institution established in 1947. For over 50 years this institution 
has been successfully promoting and nurturing the standardization 
movement in the country. It has provided for the harmonious 
development of standardization, marking and quality certification 
of goods. However, there is now a need for BIS to revitalize its 
core competencies. The existing procedures of BIS formulated 
several years ago are somewhat  shrouded in secrecy and 
confidentiality. Government is, however, committed to greater 
transparency. There is also a gr eater participation of people in 
decision making. The increased use of computers, the internet 
and websites has made it possible to reach out to people in a 
cost effective way. BIS should overhaul its procedures in the 
light of these developments and increase transparency in its 
operations. List of members of Technical Committees, draft 
standards, list of licensees and their present status may be put 
on its website and updated at monthly intervals. The possibility 
of placing test reports of samples drawn from factory or market 
on the web may also be considered. 
* In the developed countries, there is only one standard for drinking 
water and countries are expected to  ensure that all drinking water 
for human consumption, whether it is made available through 
the distribution network or in containers, conforms to those 
standards. It is time that the Government/Municipal machinery 
gears itself up to provide safe drinking water through its distribution 
network. 
* There is also need to review the permissible limits of contaminants 
in other food products under PFA. This may also lead to a wider 
discussion regarding permissible le vels of use of pesticides and 
fertilizers for agriculture and hortic ulture purposes. As long as 
pesticides and fertilizers are used for agriculture, they would 
have an adverse effect on food and water. 
* A water re-charging system shoul d be made mandatory for this 
industry. Some guidelines regarding selection of sites for 
122 

[21 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
installation of packaged drinking water industry are also required 
to ensure their location in pollution free areas. 
 When BIS establishes a standard, it must specify the 
corresponding test methods. In the amended standards 
(Amendment No. 4 of February 2003) it has been stated that 'the 
analysis shall be conducted by using internationally established 
test methods meeting the residue limits specified". This is vague 
and has left the choice of method to laboratories, which will lead 
to confusion, as it will not permit comparison between the results 
of different laboratories. BIS should constitute a committee of 
Experts from the leading research institutions like Central 
Pollution Control Board (CPCB), National Institute of Nutrition 
(NIN), Central Food 'Technology  Research Institute (CFTRI), 
Central Food Laboratories, Indian Toxicological Research Centre 
(ITRC), Indian Institute of Technology (NT), National 
Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI) etc. 
engaged in evaluation of water quality for a review of the standards 
specified in IS: 13492 and IS: 14543 in order to specify the test 
methods to be followed by the testing laboratories.

3081. SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state :

training camps at Muridke in Pakistan has risen to record levels with an 
aim to fight Indian Security Forces in Jammu and Kashmir State;

Government in this regard; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a ) Pakistan has so far not taken 
any action that would indicate a long-term oriented approach to abandoning 
the use of terrorism as an instrument  of policy against India. Pakistan 
continues to support cross border terrorism through funding, training 
indoctrination, launch and guidance. 
(b) and (c) Government have repeatedly made it clear to Pakistan 
that creation of conducive environmen t for a sustained dialogue necessarily 
requires an end to cross border terrorism and dismantling of the 
infrastructure of support to terrorism in Pakistan.

Bill against India in US Congress 
3086. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the Minister 
of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a Bill has been passed by US Congress 
imposing restriction on aid to h india due to non-payment of tax for a building 
in New York; 
(b) if so, the details in this regard; and 
(c) the action being taken by Government in the matter? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) and (b) The US Congress has 
not passed such a bill till date. While considering State Department's 
Authorization Bill (S-925), Democr at Senator Charles E. Schumer from 
New York had introduced an Amendment No. 1188 titled 'Penalty for Unpaid 
Property Taxes' on July 10, 2003. It proposed that an amount equal to 
110% of the total amount of unpaid property tax owed by a foreign country 
to the District of Columbia and New York City shall be with held from the

to through voice vote by the US Senate. However, the main bill S-925 
has not been voted upon in the Senate till date.

interest thereon for the Government-owned Permanent Mission of India 
(PMI) building in New York has not been found justifiable, it is being 
contested by the Government of India in the Supreme Court of the State 
of New York.
